sections.label: Political Donations Act ported over
sections.summary: The second part of the Bill ports over and updates the existing Political Donations Act.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The second part is about slightly more than half of this Bill.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: There is existing law, the Political Donations Act (PDA), and we have ported over the existing PDA and updated it.

sections.label: Politics for Singaporeans
sections.summary: The philosophy is that Singapore politics is for Singaporeans to deal with.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The philosophy is that our politics is for Singaporeans to deal with.

sections.label: PDA rules on foreigners
sections.summary: The PDA sets out rules for interactions with foreigners for election candidates, election agents and political associations.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We say it is not for the Americans to tell us what to do, as they have tried, and it is not for anyone else to tell us what to do either.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: This was expressed in 1973 in the President's speech and expressed in law through the PDA, which sets out rules for interactions with foreigners for election candidates, election agents and political associations.

sections.label: Huang Jing expulsion 2017
sections.summary: Academic Huang Jing was expelled in 2017 for collaborating with foreign intelligence agents.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Members would be familiar with the expulsion of academic Huang Jing in 2017 for collaborating with foreign intelligence agents.

sections.label: Objective of permanent unrest
sections.summary: It specifies its objective is an environment of permanent unrest and conflict within an enemy state.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It specifies that its objective is to achieve an environment of permanent unrest and conflict within an enemy state.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It includes harnessing the protest potential of the population of a target country, deepening the divisions within that, increasing hostility among different groups and getting them to distrust institutions.

sections.label: Russia targeted Czech extremists
sections.summary: The 2018 Select Committee received evidence Russia targeted extremists and fringe politicians to spread propaganda in the Czech Republic.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Our 2018 Parliamentary Select Committee received evidence that Russia had targeted extremists and fringe politicians to spread propaganda, undermine support for Ukraine and cause one-quarter to one-third of the Czech population to believe that the Ukrainian government was fascist.

sections.label: Dutch Referendum Russian Disinformation
sections.summary: Russians posed as Ukrainians and ran an online disinformation campaign during the Dutch EU-Ukraine FTA referendum, which voted against the FTA.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: During the Dutch Referendum on the EU-Ukraine FTA, Russians pretended to be Ukrainians, inflamed local debates, supported by online disinformation campaign involving fake stories about Ukraine and Dutch voters, eventually, voted against the FTA.

sections.label: BBC 15-year Disinformation Campaign
sections.summary: In December 2020 the BBC reported a 15-year global disinformation campaign for one country, covering at least 116 countries and targeting MEPs and the UN.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In December 2020, the BBC reported on a vast 15-year global disinformation campaign to serve one particular country’s interests.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This campaign spread over at least 116 countries, more than half of the world's countries, and targeted members of the European Parliament as well as the United Nations.

sections.label: Elections and Referendums Impacted
sections.summary: Between 2015 and 2020, at least 38 elections and six referendums were impacted.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Between 2015 and 2020, at least 38 Elections and six Referendums were impacted.

sections.label: Select Committee Online Manipulation Costs
sections.summary: The 2018 Select Committee heard one million Instagram likes cost US$18, 100 Twitter likes or retweets 34 US cents, and a US street protest about US$200,000.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Select Committee in 2018 heard one million Instagram "Likes" cost US$18; to get 100 Twitter follower likes or re-tweets costs 34 US cents; and to organise a street protest in the US through online costs about US$200,000.

sections.label: Macedonia Fake News Websites
sections.summary: In the final weeks of the 2016 US Presidential Elections, over 140 fake news US politics websites traced to Macedonia overtook mainstream news producers in Facebook election stories shared.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In the final weeks of the 2016 US Presidential Elections, over 140 "fake news" US politics websites were traced to Macedonia, and these overtook mainstream news producers in their share of election stories shared on Facebook.

sections.label: Singapore Sweden Information Manipulation Resilience
sections.summary: The report said Singapore was resilient through a counter-narrative of Singaporean identity and swift reactions to hate speech, concluding Singapore and Sweden were among the best prepared against information manipulation and hybrid threats.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The report said we were resilient through a counter-narrative of our Singaporean identity and by our swift reactions against hate speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It concluded that we, along with Sweden, were one of the best prepared states in the fight against information manipulation and hybrid threats in general.

sections.label: SingHealth cyber attack and HIC
sections.summary: Hackers stole 1.5 million patients' particulars from SingHealth in 2018, and a coordinated HIC occurred during 2016-2017 tensions with another country.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In the cyber attack in 2018, hackers targeted SingHealth’s databases and stole the particulars of 1.5 million patients, including the Prime Minister's data.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: During a period of tension with another country between 2016 and 2017, we experienced a coordinated HIC that attempted to undermine our foreign policy position.

sections.label: Foreign interference in elections
sections.summary: Experts testified on alleged Russian interference in the 2016 US and 2017 French elections, and noted Singapore's vulnerability when race and religion are used.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Disinformation expert, Mr Ben Nimmo, testified on the Internet Research Agency (IRA)'s various tactics, said to be controlled by Russia, tactics to boost support for Mr Trump, as he then was, and opposition to Mrs Clinton during the 2016 US Presidential Elections and to widen the divide in the US between the Black Lives Matter movement and the Police.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Dr Kevin Limonier, a French cybersecurity expert, spoke of an alleged Russian HIC that tried to sway the 2017 French Presidential Elections using a combination of state media, social media platforms and bots, including by attempting to spread leaked emails on the eve of the election to discredit the Macron campaign.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Experts also highlighted that Singapore has been targeted and is especially vulnerable when race and religion are used as an issue of protest potential.

sections.label: SAF and internet as theatre
sections.summary: The SAF is well-regarded for professionalism, technology and interoperability, but Dr Raska said the Internet is an attractive theatre for adversaries.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) is very well-regarded both in the region and globally for its professionalism, technological edge and the interoperability of our systems – what Mr Lee Kuan Yew said, the vision of a "poisoned shrimp".

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But what that means, as Dr Raska pointed out, is that the Internet becomes a particularly attractive theatre for our adversaries who would seek to do us harm.

sections.label: Select Committee recommended measures
sections.summary: The Select Committee recommended measures be taken, and Parliament was told legislation will be considered and will be necessary.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Select Committee recommended that measures be taken and we have said in Parliament that legislation will be considered and legislation will be necessary.

sections.label: FICA misinformation and CPC
sections.summary: Misinformation claims FICA would give the Government new powers to get any information, but Section 20 of the CPC has been used for investigations.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: One of the pieces of misinformation that are being put out is that the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act, or FICA, would now allow the Government to get any information and that this is a new power.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Section 20 of CPC has been used all these years and it is in broad terms to get any information for investigations.

sections.label: FICA directions and prosecution
sections.summary: Under FICA, directions can be given for foreign-principal online activity in the public interest, and offenders prosecuted, but there is no detention without trial.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If FICA is passed, then we can proceed under FICA if we can show that online communications activity has been prepared or planned, by or on behalf of a foreign principal, and it is in the public interest to give one or more directions.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The person can also be arrested and prosecuted if an offence of clandestine foreign interference is made out.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But under FICA, there is no detention without trial.

sections.label: FICA Proscribed Online Locations App Removal
sections.summary: The digital equivalent under FICA is a Proscribed Online Locations App Removal.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The digital equivalent under FICA is a Proscribed Online Locations App Removal.

sections.label: FICA update on online HICs
sections.summary: FICA updates laws to deal with online HICs through platform disclosure and new offences proved beyond reasonable doubt in Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Today, you see the existing powers of investigation and of arrest and detention, in light green.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It can be seen that FICA is an update to ensure that our laws can deal with online HICs, by allowing for disclosure of information by global platforms, and new offences which have to be proved beyond reasonable doubt in Court for perpetrating HICs in a clandestine way.

sections.label: FICA measures for designated PSPs
sections.summary: Under FICA, a designated PSP first faces annual declaration of donations, with other measures applied by the Competent Authority if foreign interference threat heightens.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Under FICA, at the first instance, the only measure that applies to a designated PSP is in the first red box in the second column which is annual declaration of donations.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If there is heightened threat of foreign interference, then, the other red boxes can be applied by the Competent Authority.

sections.label: FICA directions to tech companies
sections.summary: Under FICA, directions can be issued to tech companies to disable access to content or restrict accounts from Singapore end users if thresholds are met.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Under FICA, directions can be issued to tech companies to disable access to the content or restrict those accounts from view of end users in Singapore, if the thresholds are met.

sections.label: Public Interest test and proportionality
sections.summary: The Public Interest test requires proportionality from the Minister before a Part direction, with necessary or expedient defined in clause 7.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The "Public Interest" test imports a built-in requirement of proportionality for the Minister before deciding on a Part   direction.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The definition of "Public Interest" refers to "necessary or expedient"; that is clause 7.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, if a decision has to be made on the basis of "necessary or expedient", you have got to look at the facts carefully and the actions you want to take must be proportional.

sections.label: Foreign collaboration not a trigger
sections.summary: Collaboration and partnership with a foreign person, by itself, is not the trigger.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Collaboration and partnership with a foreign person, by itself, is not the trigger.

sections.label: Legislative intent and AGC advice
sections.summary: The speaker says he forms his own views but follows AGC advice, and states the Bill's legislative intent will guide its interpretation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I am capable of forming my own views but we go by the advice of AGC.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And this is the intent behind the legislative approach which we are setting out clearly for reference, so that if this Bill becomes law, and if it needs to be interpreted, it will be interpreted in the light of what the Government has said is the legislative intent and how the phrases are intended to cover these things.

sections.label: Suggestion on open collaboration
sections.summary: One suggestion was that open non-clandestine collaboration between Singaporeans and an ordinary private foreign citizen to improve laws or policies constitutes foreign interference.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: One suggestion was open non-clandestine collaboration between Singaporeans and any ordinary private foreign citizen to improve any aspect of our laws and public policies constitutes foreign interference, notwithstanding the absence of any foreign state manipulation or foreign funding.

sections.label: Foreigners exchanging viewpoints with Singaporeans
sections.summary: Groups of foreigners exchanging viewpoints with Singaporeans are not covered, but political change motives, money or materiality make it different.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There could be a group of foreigners working with Singaporeans, exchanging viewpoints, writing papers and so on, we have indicated that that would not be covered.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But, supposing, the group comes together and the motive is to effect a change; or take a different example, there is money involved or, let us say, there is materiality, and the entire focus is political change; then, again, Members of Parliament will say that is a very different kettle of fish.

sections.label: Academic activities and FICA coverage
sections.summary: Foreign-funded academic activities described will not fit within FICA, but becoming an agent of influence or an orchestrated campaign becomes different.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Another point that has been made is that presenting research at overseas conferences, writing for international journals, multi-authored book projects, publishing in and reviewing for prestigious academic presses, participating in international collaborative research projects, partaking of fellowships, visiting appointments, training programmes, participation in international funding opportunities, any of these may be subsidised or fully funded by foreign universities, foundations and states.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: None of that, on the face of it, as it is described, will fit within FICA, for the reasons I have already explained.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But if there is a step-up to try and turn the person into an agent of influence, or there is an orchestrated campaign, then, again, it becomes different.

sections.label: Difficulty of identifying foreign interference
sections.summary: MHA and many countries face the difficulty that out of 10,000 interactions, one might be an attempt to interfere.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The difficulty we face at MHA, and which many other countries face when dealing with this foreign interference issue, is that out of 10,000 interactions, one might be the sort that we are interested in, where there is an attempt to interfere.

sections.label: ACRA rejected OSF-funded company
sections.summary: In 2018, ACRA rejected Thum and Han's attempt to register an OSF-funded company to organise democracy classroom sessions in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In 2018, ACRA rejected Thum and Han's attempt to register a company funded by OSF to organise "democracy classroom" sessions in Singapore.

sections.label: Han on social movements
sections.summary: Han described a social movement as work toward potentially having 500,000 people on the streets, said foreigners should not be barred from influencing domestic affairs, and holds that Malaysians can influence Singapore politics.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Han described a social movement as "the work that goes into potentially one day having 500,000 people on the streets." She has also said, "When the government says foreigners should not influence domestic affairs, or foreigners should not bring their country's politics into Singapore, we should push back on that as well, because why not, because solidarity is important." Her view is that Malaysians can influence our politics.

sections.label: Han on foreign funding
sections.summary: Han argued against the Bill that money for these causes is difficult to get in Singapore, so foreign funding is necessary.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Han has said, in arguing against this Bill, that it is difficult to get money for these causes in Singapore, so foreign funding is necessary.

sections.label: FICA transparency and HIC appeals
sections.summary: FICA allows a transparency directive requiring Singaporeans be told upfront the article's author and nationality, and HIC direction appeals go to an independent reviewing tribunal that can overrule the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: FICA will allow us to issue a transparency directive requiring that Singaporeans be told upfront who the article is written by and what nationality the author has.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: For HIC directions, appeals go to an independent reviewing tribunal, which has the power to overrule the Minister.

sections.label: Workers' Party on foreign interference
sections.summary: The Workers' Party stated it believes in the legitimate need to counter malign acts of foreign interference.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Workers' Party has stated that they believe in the "legitimate need to counter malign acts of foreign interference".

sections.label: CEC members left out
sections.summary: One reason CEC members were left out is that CEC members as well as branch secretaries were considered for inclusion.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: On the CEC members, one of the reasons why we left it out is that we did consider CEC members as well as branch secretaries to be included.

sections.label: Rules for DSes and PSes
sections.summary: DSes and Permanent Secretaries are subject to various tight rules and requirements tighter than FICA requirements on PSPs.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: What is the status of DSes and Permanent Secretaries (PSes) and what rules are they subject to?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They are all subject to various tight rules and requirements which are tighter than FICA requirements on PSPs.

sections.label: Anonymous donation thresholds for PSPs
sections.summary: PSPs cannot accept anonymous donations over $5,000, but may accept anonymous donations under $5,000 and above $5,000 from identified persons.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: PSPs cannot accept anonymous donations over $5,000, which really means they can accept anonymous donations under $5,000 and they can also accept above $5,000 from identified persons.

sections.label: Senior civil servants as PSPs
sections.summary: The speaker says it is not appropriate to classify senior civil servants as PSPs because they are non-political, so the proposal cannot be agreed.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I also do not think it is appropriate to classify them as PSPs.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: These senior civil servants are non-political, so, we cannot agree to this proposal.

sections.label: First five political purposes
sections.summary: The first five purposes are promoting a political party's interests, influencing elections or referendums, Governmental decisions, public institution proceedings, and law or legislative process changes.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: For those of us who cannot read this slide, the first five are: (a) to promote the interests of a political party, or a politically significant entity, in Singapore; (b) to seek to influence the outcome of any election or referendum; (c) to seek to influence Singapore Governmental decisions, including by trying to influence the public; (d) to seek to influence any aspect of proceedings of key public institutions, including Parliament, Presidential Council for Minority Rights, and so on; (e) to seek to bring about changes of the law or otherwise influence the legislative process.

sections.label: HIC and PSP designation conditions
sections.summary: HIC directions require three conditions and PSP designations two; under Mr Gerald Giam's proposal, issues only within (f) or (g) would allow no counter-HIC directions or PSP designation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Members will recall that I have said a number of times that there are three conditions for a HIC direction and two for a PSP designation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: For HIC directions, to refresh Members' memory, there has to be online activity where material is published in Singapore, it has to be done on behalf of a foreign principal and public interest in Singapore is likely to be affected.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: For a PSP designation, the person's or entity's activities must be directed wholly or in part towards a political end; and the Competent Authority must additionally assess that it is in the public interest for countermeasures to be applied.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: With Mr Gerald Giam's proposal, if an issue is only within (f) or (g), then no counter-HIC directions can be issued and no PSP designation is possible.

sections.label: Deletions may fall outside FICA
sections.summary: With Mr Gerald Giam's deletions, such conduct may fall outside FICA, allowing foreign interference and manipulation with no offence and no Part 3 directions.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: With the deletions that Mr Gerald Giam has proposed, such conduct may fall outside of FICA, unless it can be referred back to one of the earlier limbs.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think it is not acceptable for us to allow such foreign interference and allow such manipulation of Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The shareholders of the sham company may even get paid for their actions and there would be no offence and no Part 3 directions can be issued, however pervasive the online campaign.

sections.label: Exemptions proposed by Jamus Lim
sections.summary: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim proposes exempting Singaporeans discussing politics and foreign individuals or publications reporting openly, both modelled on the Ministry's 13 September 2021 press release.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In this context, let us also look at the exemptions proposed by Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: He proposes to exempt "any activity undertaken by Singaporeans to exercise their right to discuss politics by expressing their own views on political matters, unless they are agents of a foreign principal".

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Second, he proposes to exempt "an activity undertaken by foreign individuals or foreign publications reporting or commenting on Singapore politics, in an open, transparent and attributable way, even if their comments may be critical of Singapore or the Government".

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Both proposals are modelled on my Ministry's press release of 13 September 2021, which was issued after the First Reading of the Bill, where we set out the powers under the Bill and explained that it will not apply to these two situations, in the context of clause 120.

sections.label: Narrowing mental state for foreign principal offence
sections.summary: The proposed amendment narrows the mental state so the prosecution must prove a person knew the publication would likely be prejudicial to Singapore's interests.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The current wording is that: "the offence is committed if A publishes in Singapore, he does this on behalf of a foreign principal and A has reason to believe that what is published is likely to be prejudicial to Singapore's interests, in one of various ways and he does this covertly and deceptively".

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Again, for those who cannot read it, you can look at the handout in the grey file that has been handed out.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This proposed amendment will narrow the mental state.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If this edit goes through, the prosecution must then prove that a person knew that it would likely be prejudicial.

sections.label: Acting covertly for foreign agency
sections.summary: Acting covertly for a foreign agency with reason to believe actions would prejudice Singapore's interests should be an offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Common sense is, if you had reason to believe that your actions are likely to prejudice Singapore's interests and you are acting for a foreign agency, you are acting covertly, secretly, it should be an offence.

sections.label: Reasonable suspicion and FICA measures
sections.summary: The speaker says action must be possible on reasonable suspicion, and under FICA the Government could issue takedown or must-carry directions.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, if a foreign publication strongly attacks a Government policy and a local person is actively helping them and pushes out that content while accepting donations from them and taking effort to conceal the funding, consistently, over time, circumstances look suspicious, but nothing can be done if we cannot prove that the person was actually acting on behalf of a foreign principal.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think we must be able to act on reasonable suspicion, which is a threshold well-established in law.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Under FICA, the Government would be able to take some measures: issue directions to take down the harmful content, or a must-carry direction to inform the public that a HIC is going on and these are executory in nature.

sections.label: Legal standard for actionable intelligence
sections.summary: The passage questions the legal standard for actionable intelligence and notes Ms He Ting Ru's proposed amendment to replace the tribunal with High Court proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There is another problem which lawyers will understand – what is the legal standard for actionable intelligence?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It will replace "suspects or has reason to believe", which is a concept which lawyers know and is well-defined; at least, there is case law.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Essentially, the tribunal will have the right to consider the information available, which the Government makes available, and decide whether the conclusion that the Government has come to was justified.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Clause 104, an amendment proposed by Ms He Ting Ru.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: She wants to replace the tribunal with proceedings in the High Court.

sections.label: Tribunal headed by Supreme Court Judge
sections.summary: A Tribunal headed by a Supreme Court Judge can overrule the Minister, while Courts ensure procedural compliance and proper exercise of jurisdiction but do not review merits.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, the theory has to fit the practice.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That is why we thought long and hard, and then, said let us have a Tribunal headed by a Supreme Court Judge who can overrule the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Courts still have a role to play and that is in the Explanatory Statement.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They will ensure procedural compliance, proper exercise of jurisdiction, but they will not review the merits, other aspects of executory decisions taken under the Bill.

sections.label: Finality of orders and decisions
sections.summary: All orders and decisions of the President and the Minister, and the Council's recommendations, are final and not subject to judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: All orders and decisions of the President and the Minister, and the recommendations of the Council, are final and not subject to judicial review.

sections.label: Immigration Act judicial review limits
sections.summary: Section 39A of the Immigration Act bars judicial review of Minister or Controller decisions except for procedural compliance.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If you look at the Immigration Act, section 39A, no judicial review for any decision made by the Minister or Controller under the Immigration Act, save in relation to procedural compliance.

sections.label: Work pass decisions and ISA detention
sections.summary: Controller work pass decisions are not subject to judicial review except for procedural compliance, and the ISA provides for detention without trial by Executive Order.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Decisions of the Controller relating to the issuance or cancellation of work passes, variation of its conditions, these are not subject to judicial review, save in relation to procedural compliance.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Internal Security Act (ISA) has been instrumental in ensuring our safety and security.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It provides for detention without trial, on Executive Order.

sections.label: Teenagers picked up recently
sections.summary: In the last couple of years, two teenagers were among those picked up.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In the last couple of years, amongst those picked up were two teenagers.

sections.label: GLOBSEC study on France attacks
sections.summary: GLOBSEC examined 22 terror incidents in France since 2012, finding most attackers were on watchlists or radar, and says the ISA could have avoided 97%.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The global security think- tank GLOBSEC examined 22 terror incidents in France since 2012 and noted that nearly 80% of the people behind those attacks had been on a terror watchlist and 97% had been on the radar of authorities.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: With the ISA, 97% of those incidents could have been avoided and many lives saved.

sections.label: Gitmo prisoner transferred for prosecution
sections.summary: To date, only one Gitmo prisoner has been transferred to the US for prosecution in federal courts, though this may be wrong.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: To date, what we can check – we may be wrong – is that only one Gitmo prisoner has been transferred to the US for prosecution in the federal courts.

sections.label: FICA directives and tribunal appeals
sections.summary: Under FICA, Executive Order directives can be issued for transparency, and a tribunal headed by a Supreme Court Judge can consider appeals under section 92.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Also, how do you have a Court process without leaks?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, if you look at what can be done through Executive Order under FICA, directives can be issued for greater transparency.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And also, it is not as if it is either a Court process or nothing.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There is a tribunal, fully empowered, headed by a Supreme Court Judge, and they can consider any appeal brought under section 92.

sections.label: Tribunal headed by Supreme Court Judge
sections.summary: It can be looked at by a tribunal headed by a Supreme Court Judge.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Second, it can be looked at by a tribunal headed by a Supreme Court Judge.

sections.label: Risk of not giving power
sections.summary: Not giving the power or requiring a Court process will severely compromise the Government's ability to deal with the real risk of foreign interference which has actually happened.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The risk of not giving the power or requiring a Court process, in the context of the risks I have outlined, will severely compromise the Government's ability to deal with the real risk of foreign interference which has actually happened.

sections.label: Bill balances risks and checks
sections.summary: The Bill represents the best balance between dealing with the risks and providing checks against abuse.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Bill represents the best balance that we can find between dealing with the risks and providing checks against abuse.

sections.label: Protection for enforcement officers
sections.summary: The Bill extends the same protection given to enforcement officers to a competent authority or authorised officer assisting a Police Officer, and is calibrated to act surgically against threats.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We recently amended the Police Force Act to provide that no liability shall lie personally against any enforcement officer who acts in good faith and with reasonable care in the execution of the Act or any other written law.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This provision simply extends the same protection to a competent authority or an authorised officer who assists a Police Officer in the execution of powers under the Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This Bill is a calibrated piece of legislation that enables us to act surgically against threats that have come and continue to loom over us.

sections.label: Clause 17 clandestine foreign interference offence
sections.summary: Clause 17 introduces the offence of clandestine foreign interference by electronic communications activity, with three stated elements.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Clause 17 introduces the offence of clandestine foreign interference by electronic communications activity.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: First, the person acts on behalf of a foreign principal, or on behalf of a person acting on behalf of a foreign principal.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Second, any part of the person’s undertaking or electronic communications activity is covert or involves deception.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Third, the person knows or has reason to believe that the electronic communications activity or the information or material published in Singapore is against Singapore’s public interest.

sections.label: Clause 18 aggravated offence
sections.summary: Clause 18 introduces a separate aggravated offence of clandestine foreign interference of a target using electronic communications activity.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Clause 18 introduces a separate aggravated offence of clandestine foreign interference of a target using electronic communications activity.

sections.label: Technical Assistance Direction introduced
sections.summary: Clause 36 introduces the Technical Assistance Direction to request assistance from social media, electronic, hosting and Internet access services and online location proprietors.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: To improve the Government’s ability to investigate potential HICs, clause 36 introduces the Technical Assistance Direction to request various forms of assistance from social media services, relevant electronic services, hosting services, Internet access service providers and proprietors of online locations.

sections.label: Must Carry Direction introduced
sections.summary: Clause 32 introduces the Must Carry Direction requiring recipients to publish a message about HIC content as prescribed by Regulations.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Clause 32 introduces the Must Carry Direction that will require the recipient to publish, post, display or include a message about the HIC content in a manner prescribed by Regulations.

sections.label: Stop Communication and Disabling Directions
sections.summary: Clause 30 introduces the Stop Communication (end-user) Direction and clause 31 the Disabling Direction for taking down content from Singapore end users' view.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Clause 30 introduces the Stop Communication (end-user) Direction, which will require communicators to take down information or material that is published in Singapore and to stop publishing similar material in Singapore; and clause 31 introduces the Disabling Direction, which will require relevant electronic services and social media services to take down specific content from the view of Singapore end users.

sections.label: App Removal and Proscribed Online Location
sections.summary: Clause 37 introduces the App Removal Direction, and clause 24 lets the Minister declare a Proscribed Online Location after one Part 3 direction.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Clause 37 introduces the App Removal Direction to stop the further distribution of an app to Singapore end users, if the app is being used to spread HIC content.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Clause 24 provides for the Minister to declare an online location as a Proscribed Online Location or POL, if one Part 3 direction, other than the Technical Assistance Direction, has been issued.

sections.label: Proscribed Online Location regime intent
sections.summary: The POL regime aims to reduce a POL's impact by reducing visibility, warning Singaporeans and cutting revenue, with Class 1 and Class 2 directions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: The intent of this POL regime is, hence, to reduce the impact of the POL by: firstly, reducing its visibility via advertising; secondly, warning Singaporeans to the threat posed by the POL; and thirdly, cutting off its revenue streams and preventing it from profiting from its operations.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Class 1 can be issued to Internet access service providers to disable access by every end user in Singapore to the website or service that had not complied with the direction.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Class 2 can be applied to Internet access service providers, relevant electronic services and social media services to disable access to a POL if paid content on the POL is published in Singapore or the POL fails to comply with the Must Carry (Class 4) Direction to notify Singaporean users about its POL status.

sections.label: Tribunal appeal process
sections.summary: Appeals must be submitted within 30 days of the Minister's reconsideration outcome, and the tribunal can dismiss, confirm or revoke the direction.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: The appeal to the tribunal must be submitted within 30 days from the outcome of the Minister's reconsideration.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: This tribunal can then dismiss the appeal, confirm the direction appealed against or revoke the direction.

sections.label: Reviewing tribunal and foreign interference
sections.summary: The reviewing tribunal structure recognises the need for checks and balances while protecting sensitive intelligence used to counter a HIC.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: The reviewing tribunal structure thus recognises the need for checks and balances while protecting sensitive intelligence that is relied upon to counter a HIC.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, we are facing a severe and evolving threat of foreign interference, which can be carried out online through HICs or through local proxies involved in our political processes, also known as Politically Significant Persons or PSPs.

sections.label: Bill's powers and existing laws
sections.summary: The Bill does not significantly increase substantive powers from existing laws and provides narrower, more targeted levers against HICs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: At least 18 representors spoke on the threat of foreign interference at the Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods in 2018.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: So, this is not a Bill that has come in haste.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: This Bill does not significantly increase the substantive powers from existing laws, such as the Internal Security Act, Criminal Procedure Code, Broadcasting Act and Telecommunications Act.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: In fact, a significant portion of the Bill is simply the Political Donations Act ported over.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: So, what the Bill does is to provide more targeted and calibrated levers against HICs, which are narrower than existing powers, such as in the Broadcasting and Telecommunications Act.

sections.label: Comparable foreign jurisdiction levers
sections.summary: Comparable levers exist in other foreign jurisdictions, and the Bill concerns covert activities to manipulate domestic politics, not open activities or criticisms.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: There are comparable levers and requirements in other foreign jurisdictions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: It is primarily concerned with covert and clandestine activities to manipulate our domestic politics and undermine our political sovereignty, and not open, transparent and attributable activities, transactions, relationships or even criticisms.

sections.label: Updating laws on foreign influence
sections.summary: Laws should be updated for new ways foreign actors can influence local political individuals and entities, as the PDA prohibits foreign monetary donations.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: We should update our laws to address the new ways that foreign actors can influence local political individuals and entities.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: We currently have the Political Donations Act (PDA) that prohibits political associations, as well as election candidates and their agents, from accepting monetary donations from foreign sources.

sections.label: Repeal PDA and define PSPs
sections.summary: The Bill will repeal the PDA, bring its obligations into the Bill, add countermeasures, and define Politically Significant Persons in Clause 14.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: To strengthen our safeguards, this Bill will repeal PDA, bring the existing PDA obligations into this Bill, and introduce some additional countermeasures.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Clause 14 of the Bill defines individuals and entities, who are formally involved in our political processes, as Politically Significant Persons (PSPs).

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: These are listed in the Bill and are, namely: political parties; Political Office Holders; Members of Parliament, which include elected Members of Parliament, Non-Constituency Members of Parliament and Nominated Members of Parliament; Leader of the House; Leader of the Opposition; election candidates; and election agents.

sections.label: Donation disclosure threshold
sections.summary: Donations need to be disclosed if they are $10,000 or more.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Donations need to be disclosed if they are $10,000 or more.

sections.label: Rules for defined PSPs
sections.summary: Defined PSPs cannot take donations from impermissible donors, cannot receive $5,000 or more of anonymous donations, and must keep a dedicated bank account for political donations.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: For example, defined PSPs are: (a) prohibited from receiving donations from impermissible donors, such as foreign donors and Singapore Citizens below the age of 21; (b) not allowed to receive $5,000 or more of anonymous donations; and (c) are required to maintain a dedicated bank account to hold their political donations.

sections.label: Ban on foreign volunteers
sections.summary: Clause 56 prohibits defined PSPs from accepting volunteer labour or services from foreigners.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Clause 56 prohibits defined PSPs from accepting volunteer labour or services from foreigners.

sections.label: Foreign volunteers for designated PSPs
sections.summary: Designated PSPs may accept foreign volunteers, but the Competent Authority can require reporting of foreign voluntary labour and services if foreign interference risk increases.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: For designated PSPs, there is no prohibition on foreign volunteers in the first instance.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: However, if there is an increased risk of foreign interference, clause 85(2)(b), read with clause 88, empowers the Competent Authority to require that the designated PSP report voluntary labour and services that are rendered by foreigners.

sections.label: Declaring foreign migration benefits
sections.summary: Clauses 78(3) and 78(4) require defined and designated PSP individuals to declare migration benefits granted by foreign countries.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Clauses 78(3) and 78(4) will require defined and designated PSP individuals to declare if they have been granted migration benefits by foreign countries.

sections.label: Declaring foreign political involvement
sections.summary: Clause 79 requires Singapore Citizens to declare their involvement in foreign political or legislative bodies.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Clause 79 will require Singapore Citizens to declare their involvement in foreign political or legislative bodies.

sections.label: Transparency directive on foreign authors
sections.summary: Clauses 80 to 82 let the Competent Authority issue a transparency directive requiring disclosure of foreign authors or principals for political articles concerning Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: If there is an increased risk of foreign interference, clauses 80 to 82 will allow the Competent Authority to issue a transparency directive to direct any newspaper, media outlet which includes online media, or any defined or designated PSP that publishes matters on political issues relating to Singapore, to disclose the particulars of any foreign author or foreign principal for whom or at whose direction the article or programme is published, if the article or programme is a political matter concerning Singapore.

sections.label: Scope of foreign agent coverage
sections.summary: Singaporeans or entities are not covered unless acting as foreign agents or working with foreigners to affect public interest.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Unless a Singaporean or entity is acting as a foreign agent or working with foreigners to affect our public interest, they will not be covered.

sections.label: Designating entity as PSE
sections.summary: The Competent Authority may designate an entity as a PSE if it has reason to believe the entity may receive support from a foreign state-linked agency.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: The Competent Authority has reason to believe that the entity may be receiving support from a foreign state-linked agency.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: This entity may be designated by the Competent Authority as a PSE.

sections.label: Directive prohibiting foreign donations
sections.summary: The Competent Authority may issue a directive prohibiting a PSE from receiving foreign donations if it is suspected of receiving funding from a foreign agency to organise a petition against the Government.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: For example, if the PSE is suspected to be receiving funding from the foreign agency to organise a petition against the Government calling for a change in our laws on the issue that the group is advocating for, the Competent Authority may issue a directive prohibiting the PSE from receiving foreign donations.

sections.label: Narrower than Australian US approach
sections.summary: The approach is narrower than the Australian or US approach.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Our approach is also narrower than the Australian or US approach.

sections.label: Bill not targeting legitimate groups
sections.summary: The Bill is not intended to target businesses, academic institutions, trade associations, clan associations or other cultural, religious, community or charity groups in their legitimate dealings with foreigners.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: In addition, I must point out that, contrary to what some commentators have been saying about FICA, the Bill is not intended to target businesses, academic institutions, trade associations, clan associations or other cultural, religious, community or charity groups in their legitimate dealings with foreigners.

sections.label: Firm stance against foreign interference
sections.summary: The Government has taken a firm stance against foreign interference since Independence, and the Bill ensures Singaporeans retain the freedom to decide how they govern and live.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: (In English): Mr Speaker, this Government has taken a firm stance against foreign interference since our Independence.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: This Bill ensures that Singaporeans retain the freedom to decide how we should govern our country, how we should live our lives.

sections.label: Amendments filed to Bill
sections.summary: Four MPs filed amendments to the Bill by the 27 September 2021 deadline, covering accountability, fairness, transparency and effectiveness.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Ms He Ting Ru, Mr Leon Perera, Mr Gerald Giam and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim filed amendments to the Bill on 27 September 2021 by 4:30 pm, which is the deadline for filing any amendments to Bills for this particular Sitting.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The thrust of the amendments is in four areas: accountability, fairness, transparency and effectiveness.

sections.label: Low thresholds of proof
sections.summary: Phrases like "is likely to" and "where the Minister suspects" create low thresholds of proof that could be unfairly used against entities and individuals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Phrases, such as "is likely to" and "where the Minister suspects" create low thresholds of proof that could be unfairly used against entities and individuals if power is in the wrong hands.

sections.label: Civil servants as significant persons
sections.summary: Civil servants from Deputy Secretary upwards should be designated like Politically Significant Persons as key nodes in decision-making.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: As key nodes in decision-making, civil servants from Deputy Secretary upwards, in our view, should be designated like Politically Significant Persons.

sections.label: Powers need robust oversight
sections.summary: The Government must have powers to intervene, but if broad powers against foreign interference are legislated, robust oversight mechanisms must prevent abuse.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It follows that the Government must have powers and, in some cases, even potentially intrusive powers, to intervene in the appropriate case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, if we accept that such broad-ranging, broadly defined powers should be legislated to deal with foreign interference, then this House must ensure the legislation of equally robust oversight mechanisms to prevent abuse of power.

sections.label: Court of Appeal on separation of powers
sections.summary: The Court of Appeal said the separation of powers is embodied in Articles 23, 38 and 93, and all power has legal limits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Court of Appeal observed that the separation of powers is, and I quote, "embodied in the Singapore Constitution by virtue of Article 23 (which vests the executive authority in the President and the Cabinet), Article 38 (which vests the legislative power in the President and Parliament) and Article 93 (which vests the judicial power in a system of the Courts)." The Court of Appeal also observed, and I quote again, "any society that prides itself in being governed by the rule of law, as our society does, must hold steadfastly to the principle that all power has legal limits, and the rule of law demands that the Courts should be able to examine the exercise of discretionary power." In stark contrast, the Bill before us today envisages the creation of a Reviewing Tribunal within the Executive branch with quasi-judicial powers with regard to the right of appeal against authorisation for Part 3 directions, or against the decisions of a Competent Authority.

sections.label: Appeal to High Court proposed
sections.summary: The public's reaction is noted, and an amendment to clause 104 is proposed to allow appeal to the Minister and then the High Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Many members of the public have read it carefully and I would forward that it shocks the sensitivities of many, and it goes some way to explain how this Bill has been framed and understood by the public since its First Reading three weeks ago.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We propose an amendment of clause 104 to allow, first, for an appeal to the Minister and, thereafter, to the High Court with full judicial scrutiny.

sections.label: No public consultation on Bill
sections.summary: The Government held no public consultation between Minister Josephine Teo's statement and the Bill's First Reading, so the public did not shape the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For example, what levels of transparency in funding support and leadership are appropriate and for whom." More significantly, the Minister then went on to say, and I quote, "The public has a big part in this to shape proposals and to give the eventual safeguards their stronger support.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It is the only way we can effectively deter bad foreign actors from exploiting our vulnerabilities." Let me say that again. "The public has a big part in this to shape proposals and to give the eventual safeguards their stronger support." In the six months between Minister Josephine Teo's statement and the First Reading of this Bill, the Government did not hold any public consultation on this Bill and nor can it be said that the public played a big part in shaping this Bill.

sections.label: Public feedback omitted on judicial review
sections.summary: The Government accepts the public wants greater checks and balances yet did not seek feedback on a Bill removing substantive judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Taking the words of the Minister and the GPC Chair together, it is wholly incongruous for the Government to accept that the public of today desires greater checks and balances, then omits to seek public feedback on a Bill that does away with substantive judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, I am also sure that, if asked, most Singaporeans would be in favour of our Courts acting as a check to ensure that executive power is exercised lawfully, appropriately and fairly.

sections.label: No public consultation in six months
sections.summary: In the six months from Josephine Teo's Committee of Supply statement to the Bill's First Reading, no public consultation or feedback was obtained.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For whom?" More importantly, she also said, "The public has a big part in this to shape proposals and to give the eventual safeguards their strongest support.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It is the only way we can effectively deter bad foreign actors from exploiting our vulnerabilities." In the period of six months from Mrs Josephine Teo's statement at this year's Committee of Supply, to the First Reading of this Bill last month, the Government has not conducted any public consultation about this Bill, or obtained public feedback as it is usually done.

sections.label: Contradiction over public consultations
sections.summary: It is highly contradictory for the Government to acknowledge public desire for checks and balances while avoiding consultations on a Bill limiting civil rights.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Looking at this as a statement by a Minister and a PAP member, it can be said to be highly contradictory if the Government acknowledges the desire of the people for more checks and balances but avoids public consultations on a Bill that will surely limit the civil rights of the Singaporeans, if it is passed by this Chamber and misused by the government of the day.

sections.label: French counter-disinformation campaign example
sections.summary: The report said building resilience and psychological defence is critical, and noted French awareness efforts blunted foreign disinformation in the 2017 presidential campaign.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The report said that to combat foreign interference, it is critical to build resilience, or, in our Total Defence parlance, psychological defence – by raising awareness about information manipulation in both the Government as well as amongst the public.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The paper noted that foreign campaigns to sway public opinion during the 2017 presidential campaign in France were unsuccessful.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This was because the French government created awareness about information manipulation, built strong central organisations to counter disinformation and undertook a strategy to push counter narratives that blunted the effects of disinformation, such as focusing public attention on the perpetrators.

sections.label: Spike in anonymous online comments
sections.summary: In her Committee of Supply speech, Josephine Teo spoke of a 2018 and 2019 spike in online comments critical of Singapore, many from anonymous accounts, during a bilateral spat with Malaysia.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In her Committee of Supply speech, Minister Josephine Teo spoke of a curious spike in 2018 and 2019 of online comments critical of Singapore, many from anonymous accounts, when there was a bilateral spat with Malaysia.

sections.label: Workers' Party Bill amendments
sections.summary: The Workers' Party filed amendments, saying the Bill falls short and public feedback should have been sought.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Ultimately, Singapore's survival depends on both its foreign policy principle of neutrality and reputation of openness to global trade, talent, investment and ideas." As things stand, particularly on the grounds of perception and fairness, this Bill falls short.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: That is why the four Workers' Party Members of Parliament have filed amendments to this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Public feedback should have been sought on this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Government failed to do so and does not appear minded to postpone this debate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: There is an opportunity to commit the Bill to a Select Committee for public input and to review oversight mechanisms, amongst others.

sections.label: Non-legislative foreign interference measures
sections.summary: The Government must immediately implement non-legislative measures such as public education and engagement to tackle foreign interference.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Government must also take immediate steps to implement non-legislative measures to tackle foreign interference, such as education and engagement of the public.

sections.label: Aye to Workers' Party amendments
sections.summary: The passage calls for saying "Aye" to all 44 amendments proposed by the Workers' Party.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Say "Aye" to all the 44 amendments proposed by the Workers' Party.

sections.label: Bill's new Government powers
sections.summary: The Bill gives the Government powers to deem individuals and groups politically significant and to monitor and restrict their activities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Today's Bill aims to push against this tide.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: It gives the Government new powers, first, to deem individuals and groups as politically significant and, second, to monitor and restrict these people's activities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The goal is to reduce foreign disruption of our domestic politics.

sections.label: Clandestine electronic communications offence
sections.summary: The Bill makes it an offence to undertake clandestine electronic communications activity on behalf of a foreign principal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: My second point is on what it means to act with covertness, deception or concealment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This Bill makes it an offence to undertake clandestine electronic communications activity on behalf of a foreign principal.

sections.label: Section 48 right to be heard
sections.summary: Section 48 allows individuals the opportunity to be heard before being designated a politically significant individual.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Section 48 allows individuals the opportunity to be heard before being designated as a politically significant individual.

sections.label: Written reasons for decisions
sections.summary: Written reasons should be provided in three scenarios: designation as politically significant, a decision not to hear an individual, and a Minister's appeal determination.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In addition, will the individual receive written reasons to explain decisions made by the Ministry and by the Competent Authority?

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: There are three scenarios where written reasons should be provided: one, when the Ministry designates an individual as politically significant; two, when the Competent Authority decides that it is not practicable or desirable to hear an individual before they get designated as politically significant; and three, when the Minister determines an appeal under section 101.

sections.label: PSP opposes FICA, seeks delay
sections.summary: The PSP says safeguards and transparency are needed but cannot support FICA as it stands, and calls for delay, public consultation and a Select Committee.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I believe there is a strong need to tackle foreign disruptions of our domestic politics but, at the same time, there needs to be safeguards in place and it is essential that we are fair and transparent in how we restrict the activities of fellow Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: But the PSP cannot support the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act, which I shall refer to as FICA, in its current form because of the insufficient evaluation by both parliamentarians and members of the public of its far-reaching implications.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, PSP calls upon the Government to delay the passing of the Bill, hold public consultations and appoint a Select Committee to scrutinise the Bill closely.

sections.label: FICA rushed through Parliament
sections.summary: FICA is a complex 127-section, 249-page Bill tabled on 13 September and passed barely three weeks later.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: FICA is a complex Bill with 127 sections over 249 pages and the content difficult to make sense of, even for senior lawyers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In spite of that, the Bill was only tabled at the last Parliamentary Sitting on 13 September, barely three weeks ago and we are already rushing through its passage today.

sections.label: FY2021 security spending figures
sections.summary: For FY2021, $15 billion goes to defence, $6.5 billion to home affairs and $0.5 billion to foreign affairs to protect sovereignty.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: For FY2021, we are spending $15 billion on defence; $6.5 billion on home affairs and $0.5 billion on foreign affairs, all for the purpose of upholding and protecting our sovereignty.

sections.label: FICA implications for accused persons
sections.summary: The speaker lists implications for an accused under FICA, including vague offences, no reason for arrest, undisclosed sources, non-bailable detention, no choice of counsel, trial in absence and no judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Just look at some of the frightening implications on people, on an accused person under FICA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: It is possible that you may inadvertently commit an offence because the definition of an offence is broad and vague.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: There is no need to give you a reason to arrest you and, if evidence is offered later, the Government does not need to reveal the source, and detention is non-bailable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: You cannot choose your own legal Counsel and can be tried in absence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: And to cap it all, there is no judicial review for all the actions that are taken against you.

sections.label: FY2021 security budget share
sections.summary: In FY2021, $22 billion was allocated to domestic and external security, a quarter of the total Budget.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: For example, in Financial Year 2021, $22 billion was allocated to maintain domestic and external security, accounting for a quarter of the total Budget.

sections.label: PSP seeks Bill postponement
sections.summary: PSP says the Bill should be postponed so the people and the Special Committee have time to scrutinise it thoroughly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: This is because without freedom of speech, even discussions on employment and livelihood issues could be restricted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Therefore, PSP feels that the Bill should be postponed to give the people and the Special Committee sufficient time to scrutinise it thoroughly.

sections.label: Bill scrutiny compared to POFMA
sections.summary: The Bill was tabled for Second Reading within three weeks with no public consultations or Select Committees, unlike POFMA's cross-party Select Committee.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Most of us are also receiving numerous requests for assistance from residents in dealing with the confusion of Quarantine Orders, the new Home Recovery Programme and also with pressing economic hardship suffered because of the latest round of tightened restrictions.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: And in the midst of many Singaporeans being preoccupied with such pressing concerns, this Bill has been tabled and put up for Second Reading within three weeks with no public consultations nor Select Committees convened for the purposes of scrutinising the powers that it gives the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This is in stark contrast to POFMA, where a cross-party Select Committee convened public hearings over eight days, which saw 79 individuals and organisations testify.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I also note that the Bill is 168 pages longer than the POFMA Bill and contains, on the face of it, even broader powers which should, logically, mean that more scrutiny must be given before it is passed.

sections.label: Suspected foreign interference instances
sections.summary: The passage asks how many instances of suspected foreign interference there have been in each of the last 10 years.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: How many instances of suspected foreign interference have there been in each of the last 10 years?

sections.label: Discretion in designating PSPs
sections.summary: The Bill's wide discretion to designate a Politically Significant Person risks discouraging public conversation and gives the Minister largely unfettered powers.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: As a specific example, the wide discretion allowed by the drafting of the Bill to designate who is a Politically Significant Person (PSP) runs the risk of encouraging many to step away from conversation in the public space to avoid the onerous countermeasures that come with being a designated PSP.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It will also be damaging to our standing connection to the global commons, which has recently already been called into question with concerns raised over the closure of Yale-NUS College.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It provides the Minister wide-ranging powers that are largely unfettered, with the only exception being a reviewing Tribunal that has a narrow scope.

sections.label: Reviewing Tribunal composition
sections.summary: Clause 92 provides for a Reviewing Tribunal of three Singaporeans each serving a three-year term.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Clause 92 provides for the setting up of a Reviewing Tribunal which comprises three individuals who each has to be Singaporeans and will serve a term of three years.

sections.label: Tribunal funding and rules
sections.summary: The tribunal's remuneration and expenses are paid from money provided by Parliament, while clause 99 lets the Minister make rules gazetted before being presented to Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The renumeration and expenses of the tribunal are paid for under money provided by Parliament, but the rules for tribunal proceedings are, under clause 99, made by the Minister and are only presented to Parliament after being gazetted.

sections.label: No tribunal appeals for designated persons
sections.summary: Designated Politically Significant Persons and those issued directives under Parts 5 or 6 have no route of appeal through the tribunal.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Individuals designated a Politically Significant Person under Part 4 or issued directives under Part 5 or 6 around countermeasures for foreign donors and activities that are not donor activities but may involve a foreign principal in Part 6 have no route of appeals through the tribunal.

sections.label: Restrictions on Reviewing Tribunal appeals
sections.summary: Even cases eligible to appeal to the Reviewing Tribunal face further restrictions, including clause 99(b) allowing rules to decline giving full particulars of reasons.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Second, even the small number of cases which are eligible to appeal to the Reviewing Tribunal, are subject to further restrictions, including the provision under clause 99(b) which states that the Minister may prescribe tribunal rules that enable a Reviewing Tribunal to decline to give the appellant the full particulars of the reasons why a decision was made.

sections.label: No correction of tribunal and Minister decisions
sections.summary: Decisions of the Reviewing Tribunal and the Minister are not subject to correction by any higher authority, with clause 104 purporting to oust judicial review except on procedural grounds.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Additionally, decisions of both the Reviewing Tribunal and the Minister are not subject to correction by any higher authority, especially as the proposed clause 104 purports to oust judicial review on all but procedural grounds.

sections.label: Clause 104 judicial review ouster clause
sections.summary: Clause 104 seeks to protect the Minister's FICA decisions from court review, which offends Article 93 vesting judicial power in the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Next, I turn to the proposed clause 104, which is what is known as a judicial review ouster clause.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The substance of this clause is that the Government seeks to protect the Minister’s decisions under FICA from review by the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This offends Article 93 of the Constitution, which expressly states that "judicial power of Singapore shall be vested in a Supreme Court and in such subordinate Courts as may be provided by any written law for the time being in force".

sections.label: Ouster clause bars illegality and irrationality review
sections.summary: The ouster clause does not allow Courts to consider judicial review applications of Minister and Competent Authority decisions on grounds of illegality and irrationality.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Crucially, for our purposes today, the ouster clause does not allow for the Courts to consider applications for judicial review of decisions taken by the Minister and Competent Authorities on the grounds of illegality and irrationality.

sections.label: Amendments remove judicial review ouster
