sections.summary: Checks and balances require judicious use of state powers, so the proposed amendments do away with the ouster of judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It is an important part of the checks and balances to ensure that powers are wielded judiciously by the state.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We cannot repeat enough our position that greater powers need greater oversight and it is, therefore, with this in mind that our proposed amendments do away with the ouster of judicial review.

sections.label: Bill against foreign principal interference
sections.summary: The Bill seeks to better protect Singapore from risks of foreign principal interference in domestic affairs.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In particular, the Bill seeks to better protect Singapore from the risks of foreign principal interference in our domestic affairs.

sections.label: Clause 17 electronic communications offence
sections.summary: Clause 17(1)(c)(iii) charges an individual for electronic communications prejudicial to Singapore's friendly relations with other countries.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Clause 17(1)(c)(iii) of the Bill, for example, will charge an individual with an offence if he or she engages in electronic communications that involve activity that, I quote, “is or is likely to be prejudicial to the friendly relations of Singapore with other countries”.

sections.label: Clauses 20 and 21 proof amendments
sections.summary: Amendments to clauses 20 and 21 proposed raising the proof level from suspicion or belief to evidence or actionable intelligence.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In clauses 20 and 21, amendments were proposed to raise the level of proof required: from mere suspicion or belief, to at least some degree of evidence or actionable intelligence.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This is justice on the basis of pre-crime, virtually straight out of the film "Minority Report".

sections.label: Threshold for pre-emptive actions
sections.summary: The threshold to engage must be evidence or actionable intelligence and a reasonable assessment of imminent harm.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: To be clear, the world can be an unpleasant place and there may well be instances where the risk of subsequent malicious activity would justify the execution of pre-emptive actions that would preclude the possibility of even more insidious outcomes.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: But the threshold for us to engage must, at least, be one where we possess evidence or, as we called for in the amendments to this Bill, actionable intelligence and a reasonable assessment of imminent harm.

sections.label: MHA social media foreign influence example
sections.summary: MHA cited an abnormal spike in online comments critical of Singapore, while Facebook executives stated no coordinated foreign inauthentic behaviour since 2017.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In the press release accompanying the First Reading of this Bill, MHA cited the example of "an abnormal spike in online comments critical of Singapore on social media in late 2018 and 2019".

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Yet, two executives at one major social media platform, Facebook, have publicly stated that it has uncovered no cases of coordinated, inauthentic behaviour by foreigners targeting Singapore since 2017.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Given the apparent contradiction, would MHA share with this House why it believed that social media activity during that period was foreign influence?

sections.label: Singaporeans lost money to con-men
sections.summary: In the first half of this year, Singaporeans collectively lost $168 million to con-men.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In the first half of this year, Singaporeans collectively lost a total of $168 million to con-men.

sections.label: Workers' Party balance proposal
sections.summary: The Workers' Party says it is better to remove ambiguous language and subject cases backed by actionable intelligence to judicial scrutiny.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The Workers' Party believes that it is far better to strike the balance between efficiency and accountability by eliminating the most ambiguous language from the law while subjecting cases corroborated by actionable intelligence to judicial scrutiny.

sections.label: K Shanmugam on foreign engagement
sections.summary: Minister K Shanmugam said politicians and parties may engage foreign parties but cannot take money from them.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In his response to Parliamentary Questions filed by then Nominated Members of Parliament Anthea Ong and Walter Theseira on foreign influence, Minister K Shanmugam explained that there is nothing to prevent politicians or political parties from engaging with foreign parties but you cannot take money from them.

sections.label: Clause 5(3) knowledge test
sections.summary: Clause 5(3) covers activities where both the person and foreign principal knew or expected the activity would or might be undertaken.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: For example, clause 5(3) states that activities will be covered as long as "both the person and the foreign principal knew or expected that the person would or might undertake such an activity".

sections.label: Foreign business and political definitions
sections.summary: The existing definitions of foreign business and foreign political organisation could cover perfectly innocuous ties.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: While we do not wish to constrain the Government's ability to act on a wide range of potential actors, the existing definitions of "foreign business" and "foreign political organisation" could encapsulate perfectly innocuous ties.

sections.label: Assurances written into law
sections.summary: The purpose is to write assurances into law, despite clause 105(5) and language criminalising diminution of Government.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The purpose is to ensure that these assurances are actually written into the law.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This is notwithstanding how clause 105(5) does provide accommodation for this by stating that competent authorities "must not exercise any power under this Act for the purpose of furthering or harming the interest of any particular political party".

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Yet, there is, simultaneously, language in the Bill that will criminalise the "diminution" of Government.

sections.label: Jamus Lim on FICA concerns
sections.summary: Jamus Lim says FICA as written is likely to be inadvertently detrimental to public interest amid cross-border relationships.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, if you can wrap up.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: This month, as we debate how to manage threats from foreign interference, we must, likewise, not lose sight of the bigger picture, one where our people, companies and policymakers are deeply and inevitably embedded in the rich mesh of cross-border relationships.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: I suspect and have reason to believe that FICA, as it is written, is likely to be inadvertently detrimental to our public interest.

sections.label: Select Committee on Online Falsehoods
sections.summary: The speaker cites their experience on the 2018 Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods, which considered 169 written representations and heard from 65 individuals and organisations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: We might sometimes think we are exercising free will, when we are mere catspaws.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: I speak today with some experience of POFMA, having been a member of the Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods which was formed in January 2018.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: So, that is more than three years ago, where we considered 169 written representations and oral evidence from 65 individuals and organisations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Some of these were shared by the Minister earlier in his speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: There were also public hearings held from 14 to 29 March 2018.

sections.label: Edwin Tong foreshadows foreign interference Bill
sections.summary: In 2019, then Senior Minister of State for Law Edwin Tong said the Government was considering legislation against foreign interference.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In 2019, then Senior Minister of State for Law Mr Edwin Tong foreshadowed this Bill when he said that the Government was considering legislation against foreign interference.

sections.label: Evidence of state-sponsored information operations
sections.summary: The Select Committee received evidence, including through private hearings, that state-sponsored information operations have been carried out against Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: The Select Committee also received evidence, including through private hearings, that state-sponsored information operations have been carried out against Singapore.

sections.label: FICA reach and thresholds
sections.summary: FICA does not increase the law's reach in substance but provides a targeted adaptor, has a high threshold, and is not more authoritarian than similar laws such as those in the United States.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: FICA does not increase the reach of the law in substance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: It merely provides the adaptor allowing the law to operate in a more targeted and precise manner.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In this way, its reach is narrower and would, in fact, increase freedoms.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: FICA is not more authoritarian than other similar laws, for example, those in the United States now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: FICA is a sword that stays in its sheath most of the time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: It has a high threshold which will not be awakened until activities attack the public interest of Singapore.

sections.label: Concerns about political space and discretion
sections.summary: The speaker lists three concerns: restricting political space may deter genuine individuals, organisations may need foreign collaborations, and the Minister gains extensive discretion under a broad Section 8 definition.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: How can we recognise the difference between an activist for human rights from one whose motivations are political in nature?

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I list three key concerns: one, regulating and restricting the political space further may deter genuine individuals; two, organisations may want, or even need, collaborations and support with other foreign entities to survive and thrive; three, the Minister will be granted extensive discretion, in addition to existing powers under ISA and POFMA.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Section 8 provides a very broad definition of what activities "directed towards a political end in Singapore" means.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This is of concern as any organisation engaging in such could be designated a Politically Significant Person under Part 4 of the Bill and will be subject to multiple additional requirements, such as the reporting of foreign donations and being subject to declare, and may be directed to stop taking in foreign volunteers.

sections.label: Minister's powers over donations and volunteers
sections.summary: The Bill empowers the Minister to direct a person to account for all donations, possibly return donations, and stop taking volunteers who are not Singapore Citizens.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Bill empowers the Minister to direct a person to account for all donations, possibly return donations and even stop taking volunteers who are not Singapore Citizens.

sections.label: Minister's discretion under Bill
sections.summary: The Bill gives the Minister great discretion and extensive powers, requiring trust and faith in the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This Bill equally asks for a lot of trust and faith in the Minister to do the right thing.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: There is great discretion given to the Minister on how to exercise the extensive powers under the Bill.

sections.label: Citizen vigilance and FICA assurance
sections.summary: A speaker asks the Minister to assure appropriate use of FICA so citizens can serve without undue fear.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Every citizen should be empowered to step up to be vigilant and to hold one another accountable.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: An educated population will be able to better discern right from wrong, facts from myths.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Before this Bill is passed, I ask the Minister to give us some assurance on the appropriate use of FICA, so that ordinary citizens like myself can serve and work for the betterment of Singapore, without undue fear.

sections.label: Singaporeans deciding Singapore's affairs
sections.summary: The Bill aims to ensure Singapore's affairs are decided by Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: The Bill before us today is to ensure that Singapore's affairs should be decided by Singaporeans.

sections.label: External intervention forms covered
sections.summary: The Bill covers interference through local agents and hostile information propaganda, citing a 2017 Australian senator's resignation.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Only in this way, can we independently and freely determine our future.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: There are various forms of external intervention and the new Bill covers two of them: first, the practice of interfering in internal affairs through local agents; second, hostile information propaganda.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: For instance, in 2017, an Australian senator resigned because he was found to have accepted donations from foreigners.

sections.label: Anonymous accounts spreading opposition illusion
sections.summary: Anonymous accounts with fake avatars posted online comments to create an illusion of popular opposition during bilateral tension.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: During this period, we noticed a sudden surge in online comments posted on social media from accounts with fake avatars, which were anonymous accounts that did not show the users' real faces.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Clearly, these anonymous users were attempting to create and spread the illusion of popular opposition by our own people to Singapore’s position, at a time of bilateral tension.

sections.label: FICA and politically significant persons
sections.summary: FICA strengthens and publicises management measures for politically significant individuals and organisations, and does not target ordinary people.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: First, the Foreign Interference Countermeasures Act (FICA) will strengthen existing management measures for politically significant individuals and organisations and also make them public.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Since foreign influence is often covert and executed secretly through proxies, the way to deal with it is to be transparent and open. "Politically significant" mainly refers to political parties, public officials, Members of Parliament and other people who have influence on national policies, as well as those individuals and organisations who are classified as "politically significant." This Bill does not target ordinary people.

sections.label: Politically significant persons foreign donations
sections.summary: Individuals or organisations with political goals may be listed as politically significant but can still accept foreign donations if funding is transparent.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: However, we also cannot rule out the possibility that some individuals and organisations whose main activities involve political goals and public interests, may be under the influence of foreign powers and may harm Singapore’s interests.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: These individuals or organisations may also be listed as "politically significant." Even if they are listed as "politically significant", they can still accept foreign donations, provided that their source of funding is transparent.

sections.label: Disclosure of political titles
sections.summary: Titles directly involving political positions must be disclosed, and the Bill aims to prevent foreign interference and protect Singapore's interest.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Where these titles directly involve political positions, they would need to be disclosed.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: The purpose of this Bill is to prevent foreign interference and protect Singapore’s interest.

sections.label: Independent tribunal for appeals
sections.summary: The Bill proposes an independent tribunal, including a Supreme Court judge and security and technology experts, to hear appeals instead of the High Court.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: The Bill proposes to establish an independent tribunal to hear appeals.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Compared with the High Court, it is more appropriate for appeals to be heard by the tribunal as this includes a Supreme Court judge and others who have expertise in the security and technology sectors.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: The members of the independent review tribunal have the necessary expertise and security clearances to deliberate on issues concerning our national security.

sections.label: Preventing hostile information campaigns
sections.summary: One of the Bill's two main features is to prevent hostile information campaigns.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: One of the two main features of the Bill is to prevent hostile information campaigns.

sections.label: Public feedback on Bill
sections.summary: The speaker was a committee member, and nearly 200 people submitted written feedback after the public was invited to do so.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: I was also a member of the committee then.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: We invited the public to submit feedback and nearly 200 people submitted written feedback.

sections.label: Fake accounts criticising Singapore
sections.summary: In December 2018, during tense bilateral relations with a neighbouring country, fake-avatar accounts posted online comments critical of Singapore to create an illusion of popular opposition.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: In December 2018 when bilateral relations between Singapore and a neighbouring country became tense, we noticed a surge in online comments posted on social media from accounts with fake avatars, and the comments were all critical of Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: They were attempting to create an illusion of popular opposition by our own people to Singapore's position.

sections.label: Foreign interference damage timing
sections.summary: The speaker says foreign interference can be wide-ranging and deeply damaging, and acting only after damage is done is too late.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: (In Mandarin):   I have already mentioned that the impact of foreign interference can be wide-ranging and deeply damaging.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: If we only act after the damage has been done, then it is too late.

sections.label: FICA broad sweeping measures
sections.summary: The disquiet stems from FICA enacting many broad and sweeping measures to prevent Singaporeans being misled by hostile information campaigns online.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The root of this disquiet is that FICA enacts many broad and sweeping measures in an attempt to prevent Singaporeans from being misled by hostile information campaigns over the Internet.

sections.label: Bill and elite capture
sections.summary: The Bill does not provide enough countermeasures against elite capture, described as clandestine foreign lobbying of influential Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Bill does not provide enough countermeasures against elite capture, which is the clandestine foreign lobbying of Singaporeans holding positions of influence.

sections.label: Amendments to codify assurances
sections.summary: Assurances are not in the letter of the law, so Jamus Lim tabled amendments to clause 120 and amendments to remove subsections F and G under clause 8.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But these assurances are not in the letter of the law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This is why the Member of Parliament for Sengkang, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, tabled amendments to clause 120, to codify MHA's assurances in this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I tabled amendments to subsections F and G under clause 8 to be removed.

sections.label: US Foreign Agents Registration Act
sections.summary: The US has the Foreign Agents Registration Act, enacted in 1938, requiring agents of foreigners to register or risk federal prosecution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The US has the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) enacted in 1938, which requires agents of foreigners to register or risk prosecution under federal law.

sections.label: Amendments adding defined PSPs
sections.summary: Malign foreign actors could co-opt local elites, so amendments were tabled to add classes of people to defined PSPs under clauses 14 and 78.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This could make it easier for malign foreign actors to co-opt local elites to use their influence either wittingly or unwittingly for the benefit of foreign powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This is why I tabled the amendments to the Bill to add several more classes of people to the list of defined PSPs under clauses 14 and 78.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: My proposed additions to the list include Permanent Secretaries (PSes) and Deputy Secretaries (DSes) in Government Ministries.

sections.label: Temasek, GIC, MAS, CPF leaders
sections.summary: The list includes board members and chief executives of Temasek, GIC, MAS and CPF Board, who direct policies and long-term asset allocations involving national reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Our list also includes the board members and chief executives of Temasek, GIC, MAS and CPF Board.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: These individuals provide directions on policies and long-term asset allocations that involve hundreds of billions of dollars of our national reserves.

sections.label: Expanded PSP list scrutiny
sections.summary: The expanded list of defined PSPs does not cover everyone who can influence policies but adds scrutiny of Government elites' interactions with foreign principals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: While this expanded list of defined PSPs does not cover every possible person who can influence policies, it provides for additional scrutiny over interactions between Government elites and foreign principals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It will require them to disclose foreign affiliations, reportable arrangements and migration benefits with foreign principals, all of which have the potential to colour their decisions on domestic and foreign policies, which affect all Singaporeans.

sections.label: Foreign influence reporting examples
sections.summary: Foreign influence operations in Australia, Sweden and the US came to light through investigative reporting, and the PAP Government has rejected the press as a fourth estate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Many incidents of foreign influence operations in other countries like Australia, Sweden and the US came to light because of investigative reporting by their free press.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: A former US National Security adviser resigned after journalists investigated and reported about his contacts with Russia.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Sweden's ambassador to China was recalled and investigated after the daughter of a Chinese-Swedish bookseller, jailed in China, made a blog post, which was reported in the media revealing that the ambassador had commissioned businessmen to negotiate a sensitive case involving her father without the knowledge of the Swedish ministry of foreign affairs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The PAP Government has rejected the notion of the press being the fourth estate which scrutinises the actions of public officials and public institutions in the public interest, calling for accountability for their actions.

sections.label: Elite capture prevention shortfall
sections.summary: In preventing elite capture, the Bill falls short compared to foreign lobbying laws in other countries.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Yet, in the area of preventing elite capture, it falls short, compared to foreign lobbying laws in other countries.

sections.label: Two fundamental principles
sections.summary: Singaporeans can agree that Singaporean politics must be decided by Singaporeans alone and that discourse must be open, transparent and accountable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: There have been many discussions on this Bill outside this Chamber.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: However, I think, as Singaporeans, all of us can agree on the following two fundamental principles: first, that Singaporean politics must be determined and decided by Singaporeans alone; second, Singaporeans all want open and transparent discourse in politics, one that is accountable to Singaporeans and not motivated or interfered in a covert or deceptive manner.

sections.label: Concern over Jamus Lim amendments
sections.summary: The speaker fears Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's amendments may blunt the Act's protection and weaken civil servants' steps against covert foreign interference.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Against this backdrop, I am concerned about the amendments proposed by Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim as I fear that in actual reality and practice, these amendments may potentially blunt the protection under the Act and weaken the steps that our civil servants can take to protect Singapore and Singaporeans from covert foreign interference.

sections.label: Mental state of mind offences
sections.summary: The speaker argues that requiring actual knowledge would be hard to prove and could weaken protection of national interests, so knowledge should be pegged to an objective standard of likelihood.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: On the proposal to amend the mental state of mind in the offences to require actual knowledge, it would be difficult to prove that a person actually knows that his action is prejudicial to Singapore’s national interests.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: This may have the unintended effect of weakening the protection of our national interests under the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Such knowledge or belief must be pegged, I think, to an objective standard of likelihood which any reasonable person ought to have in the circumstances, which is what the current wording in the Bill suggests.

sections.label: Minister's anticipatory directions powers
sections.summary: The speaker says he understands that the urgency and covert nature of foreign interference may require action based on reasonable suspicion, a standard well established in law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In relation to the powers of the Minister to issue anticipatory directions, I can understand that given the urgency and covert nature of foreign interference, the authorities may require action to be taken on the basis of reasonable suspicion, which is a standard well established in law.

sections.label: Reviewing Tribunal and judicial proceedings
sections.summary: The speaker asks what measures will ensure Reviewing Tribunal proceedings conclude expeditiously and what safeguards ensure confidentiality of national security information, suggesting MHA consider periodic reports on FICA offences or directions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Fourth, on the Reviewing Tribunal and judicial proceedings, clause 112 makes every offence in Part 3 arrestable and non-bailable and the rest of the offences arrestable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In this regard, what are the measures that will be in the subsidiary legislation or otherwise to ensure that the Reviewing Tribunal proceedings can be concluded expeditiously?

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Also, given that such proceedings will touch on matters of national security and interests, what are the safeguards in place to ensure the confidentiality and secrecy of the information or any evidence produced in those proceedings, whether under the Official Secrets Act (OSA) or other applicable legislation?

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I can understand that full disclosure would be extremely sensitive to the mission success of any intelligence operations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: However, perhaps MHA can consider, from time to time, giving a report on the FICA offences or directions without the need to go into the specific details or naming the individuals or foreign principals involved.

sections.label: IRSEM study on foreign interference
sections.summary: A study by the Strategic Research Institute at the French Military College, published last week, found Singapore highly exposed to foreign interference.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In a study by the Strategic Research Institute at the French Military College, or IRSEM, which was published just last week, Singapore was found to be highly exposed to foreign interference.

sections.label: Ministry conditions and judicial review
sections.summary: The speaker says the Ministry must meet prescribed conditions before issuing an order, courts retain judicial review power, and Singapore has trusted institutions and an independent judiciary.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The Ministry must also meet the prescribed conditions before it can issue an order through this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In fact, the Court still has the power to establish a judicial review in certain cases according to the existing Court's inherent jurisdiction.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Singapore also has an excellent reputation and high degree of trust in the Police and Government, a robust legislative system and an independent judiciary.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: If an individual is truly not involved, it is very easy for him to refute the accusation with strong evidence.

sections.label: Support for the Bill
sections.summary: The speaker states that notwithstanding the clarifications, he stands in support of this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding the clarifications, I stand in support of this Bill.

sections.label: 2018 Singapore health data cyber attack
sections.summary: An MP asks how transparent the Government will be if evidence shows a foreign entity behind harmful activities against Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Of course, we all know about the biggest attack that Singapore was subject to in 2018 where the personal particulars of more than 1.5 million patients were stolen and the health records of Prime Minister Lee was also targeted specifically by hackers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: While it has never been officially reported, it was hinted, Mr Speaker, Sir, that the cyber attack then was likely to have been orchestrated by state-linked hackers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: So, my question is, if there is sufficient evidence that a foreign entity, be it a government or organisation, is behind certain activities that are deemed harmful or detrimental to Singapore, how transparent will the Government be in making that information known to Singaporeans?

sections.label: Overseas funding for NGOs clarified
sections.summary: An MP seeks clarification on the position regarding NGOs, especially local chapters of global NGOs, receiving overseas funding.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Overseas funding for Politically Significant Persons (PSPs), political parties or for organisations involved in political activities is clearly undesirable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I believe every Member of this House would agree with me broadly on this point.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: However, I would like to seek clarifications from the Minister on the position regarding NGOs, especially if these NGOs are local chapters of a global NGO.

sections.label: FICA effect on global NGO chapters
sections.summary: An MP asks whether FICA would classify such NGOs as agents of influence or forbid their overseas funding.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: With FICA in place, would these NGOs be classified as agents of influence and be ordered to cease their operations here?

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I would also like to seek clarifications on the Government’s position regarding local chapters of global NGOs that are currently receiving regular funding support from overseas donors and their parent NGOs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: With FICA, would these NGOs then be forbidden from accepting funding from those channels, thus affecting the ability of these local chapters to operate in Singapore?

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I ask this, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, because there are NGOs that might be receiving overseas funding or support that are doing work, good work, that is beneficial to Singaporeans and the Singaporean community as a whole, and we would not want them or the work they are doing to be inadvertently affected by this Bill.

sections.label: FICA spirit against foreign interference
sections.summary: An MP says FICA is useful legislation and its core spirit is protecting Singapore from foreign influences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Although not perfect, FICA is still useful legislation to help safeguard Singapore against foreign interference.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: However, we must not let the debates over the form of the Bill or partisan politics detract us from the spirit of what the Bill intends to do.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: We need to acknowledge that the core spirit of the Bill is aimed at protecting our country from foreign influences that might destabilise our society or undermine the national interests of Singapore.

sections.label: Bill gives Ruling Party more power
sections.summary: An MP says the Bill gives the Ruling Party more levers of power that can potentially be abused for partisan purposes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We should talk about bread-and-butter matters and Workers' Party Members of Parliament make parliamentary interventions on these matters even during the Sittings, such as Parliamentary Questions on COVID-19.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It is important not only because there have always been malicious foreign actors who seek to twist our politics to their own ends and always will be, it is also important because the Bill the Government has placed before Parliament today promises to give yet more levers of power to the Ruling Party, which can potentially be abused for partisan purposes, to limit criticism and disadvantage political opponents, plus corroding the very functioning of our hard-won democratic society.

sections.label: Bill fails on three counts
sections.summary: An MP says the Bill fails on insufficient oversight, Executive over-reach and overlooked policy areas, proposing High Court appeals and judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Overall, as my colleagues have elaborated on, this Bill fails on three counts, the three "overs", if I may, namely, insufficient oversight, Executive over-reach and overlooking some areas of policy where foreign interference could act, but which this Bill does not provide clear remedies for.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Leader of the Opposition and my colleague, Sengkang Member of Parliament Ms He Ting Ru, had elaborated on this and explained why we propose to allow High Court appeals and judicial review on FICA matters.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This creates the potential for abuse of power, especially when we recall that the Minister, like all Ministers regardless of party, is still a political partisan at the end of the day, with a vested interest in winning arguments over critics and opponents and winning elections.

sections.label: Foreigners influencing senior government figures
sections.summary: It overlooks that foreigners could interfere by influencing senior government figures or a Minister for Home Affairs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Thirdly, Sir, it overlooks the potential for foreigners to interfere by influencing senior government figures or even a Minister for Home Affairs himself or herself one day.

sections.label: Workers' Party amendments and speeches
sections.summary: The Workers' Party's amendments and speeches seek to address oversight, over-reach and unmet needs overlooked.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Oversight, over-reach and unmet needs overlooked are what the Workers' Party’s amendments and speeches seek to address today.

sections.label: Bill's powers and missing investigative authority
sections.summary: The Bill creates no independent investigative authority and vests broad discretionary powers with the Minister for Home Affairs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And this is a subject my hon colleague Mr Gerald Giam also spoke about.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This Bill does not create an independent investigative authority that could look into all cases of malicious FI, whether directed at the Ruling Party or the Opposition, nor does it specify a clear route of complaint and follow-up action in cases where a member of the public, be it an NGO, a researcher or an ordinary citizen, has formed suspicions that a Minister is under inappropriate foreign influence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Instead, the Bill, like other Bills in the past, vests broad discretionary powers with the Minister for Home Affairs to act against FI directed at others.

sections.label: Equal FICA application to foreigners
sections.summary: It asks whether the Minister will apply FICA directives and actions equally to foreigners intervening for the Ruling Party or Opposition.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: As I explained many times, it would be a bit like criticising Usain Bolt for not running fast enough.” To be sure, I am not calling for action to be taken against this person under FICA and I would argue for a more liberal approach towards debate in general, so long as there is transparency.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, does the Minister agree that he will apply FICA directives and actions equally to foreigners who improperly intervene in our domestic politics whether on the side of the Ruling Party or the Opposition?

sections.label: Foreigner volunteers and PA activities
sections.summary: It asks whether foreigners volunteering for the PA will be subject to foreigner volunteer reporting, and notes no deadline for reconsideration decisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Given these political connotations and corollary political effects associated with some of the PA’s activities involving Ruling Party figures, will foreigners volunteering for the PA also be subject to foreigner volunteer reporting?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This could be one route along which foreign interference directed at the Ruling Party travels.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, it appears that the Minister does not have a corresponding deadline against which he or she has to come to a decision on the application for reconsideration.

sections.label: Appeal rights for designated persons
sections.summary: Those designated as PSPs or PSEs or issued Parts 5 and 6 directives may only appeal to the Minister, not the Tribunal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Thirdly, pursuant to clause 93, those who are designated as PSPs or PSEs or issued directives under Parts 5 and 6, may only appeal against that decision to the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: They have no right of appeal to the Tribunal, unlike those who are issued Part 3 directions.

sections.label: Amendments require publicising government decisions
sections.summary: The amendments require the Government to publicise all decisions under the Bill, including reasons for designating PSPs and PSEs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The overall thrust of these amendments is to require the Government to publicise all of its decisions under this Bill, in terms of designating PSPs, issuing directives and taking other actions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The amendments also require that the Government publish the reasons why decisions are taken, including reasons for designating persons or entities, PSPs as dealt with in clause 48 or PSEs as dealt with in clause 47.

sections.label: Codifying FICA publication in law
sections.summary: The speaker argues the Government's assurance to publish FICA information should be codified in law to bind current and future governments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Fourth and, most importantly, Sir, notwithstanding the Government’s public assurance that it would publish information about FICA, we believe that this should be codified in law, so that this Government and future governments are obligated to do this under the law.

sections.label: Risks of state discretionary powers
sections.summary: The speaker says strengthening state discretionary powers diminishes education and trust, risking Executive over-reach, abuse and harmed national unity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: By staking so much on strengthening state discretionary powers in this manner, we diminish the role of education and trust in the political maturity of our citizens, who are better educated than ever.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We also risk Executive over-reach and abuse, and the risk of that over-reach or abuse diminishes trust in our institutions potentially, turns our citizens against one another potentially and harms national unity in the face of these foreign threats potentially.

sections.label: Clause 5 foreign principal definition
sections.summary: Concerns exist that clause 5 defines acting on behalf of a foreign principal too broadly, including collaboration with a foreign individual or entity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: Zooming straight into clause 5 of the Bill, there are concerns that this clause defines activities or conduct "on behalf of a foreign principal" too broadly, to include those "in collaboration with" a foreign individual or entity.

sections.label: FICA purpose narrow, tactics broad
sections.summary: The speaker states FICA's purpose against the external enemy is very narrow, though the range of tactics in the Bill is broad.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: Second, to deal with this external enemy, the purpose of FICA is, in fact, very narrow, even if the range of tactics provided for in this Bill is, indeed, quite broad.

sections.label: Australia's Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme
sections.summary: Australia's FITS covers formal or informal arrangements with foreign principals, illustrated by Company A lobbying for a foreign government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: Australia, for example, has the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme (FITS) since 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: An applicable arrangement with a foreign principal under FITS could be "formal or informal, written or verbal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: It could be a contract, understanding or agreement of any kind." As illustration, if Company A and a foreign government make plans to import Australian food into the foreign country and Company A lobbies the Australian government on export regulations, Company A is deemed to be acting "on behalf of" the foreign government, even if it is also acting for itself.

sections.label: Democratic vote as check
sections.summary: The speaker says the ultimate check on governmental powers is the democratic vote, not more legislative guard rails.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: First, and most fundamentally, we should recognise that the ultimate check and balance on governmental powers is not in more and more legislative guard rails, but rather, in the democratic vote in our own hands.

sections.label: Minister's commitment to publish
sections.summary: The speaker agrees with Mr Perera's amendments and welcomes the Minister's commitment that designations, countermeasures, transparency directives and most Part 3 Directions will be made public.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: I agree with the spirit of Mr Perera's proposed amendments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: I am heartened to hear the Minister reiterate his Ministry's commitment made to the media last week that any designation of Politically Significant Persons, any stepped-up countermeasures for these Persons, any transparency directive to publish on political matters with foreign links and any Part 3 Direction against harmful foreign online communications except for Technical Assistance Directions will be made public.

sections.label: Amendment to clause 116
sections.summary: The Minister has given notice to move an amendment to clause 116 requiring notice of every Part 3 Direction except Technical Assistance Directions, designations and directives.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: To this end, I am glad to note that the Minister has also served notice in his speech just now, to move an amendment to clause 116 itself, with the new language reading, "...it must prepare a notice informing about every Part 3 Direction except the Technical Assistance Direction given, every designation made under Part 4 or every directive given under Parts 5 or 6".

sections.label: Where Part 3 directions published
sections.summary: The speaker asks where Part 3 directions will be published, noting the Ministry mentioned a Registry for Parts 4, 5 and 6.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: One, the Ministry has mentioned a Registry of Foreign and Political Disclosures for Parts 4, 5 and 6 in its interview with the media last week.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: So, my question is, where will Part 3 directions be published?

sections.label: Assurance for youth climate activist
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister to assure the House that a youth climate activist working with regional or international friends has nothing to worry about under FICA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: This is difficult to do, as the concerns that Singaporeans may have towards the Bill can be very visceral, as I noted at the start of my speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: So, to this end, can the Minister give definitive assurance, in this House, once again, that the youth climate activist working with regional and or international friends to advance their joint vision for climate justice has nothing to worry about as regards FICA and can indeed look forward to continuing and growing his or her work?

sections.label: Debate on removing limbs (f) and (g)
sections.summary: The speaker asks Mr Giam whether removing limbs (f) and (g) would defang FICA rather than limit executive over-reach, noting the Workers' Party raised no concern in 2017.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: Mr Giam has proposed to remove limbs (f) and (g) of the definition in the Bill, namely, (f) on public opinion about a matter of public controversy in Singapore and (g) on political debate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: Now, I have listened to the Minister explain the philosophy behind clause 8 and Mr Giam's argument for the proposed omissions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: I therefore like to ask Mr Giam if he would not agree that the real effect of his proposed omissions will not so much scope the powers of the executive to limit the potential for over-reach and abuse of power but rather the real effect will be to curtail the real powers that the executive needs to counter the real and highly complex threats that FICA is exactly designed to counter?

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: Would Mr Giam not agree that his proposed omissions defang FICA and strip it of its basic effectiveness to fight foreign interference?

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: In that debate in 2017, the Workers' Party had expressed no concern about the very same definition.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: So, it is not clear to me why the Workers' Party would have a concern now about the same definition four years on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
sentences.text: I believe I actually explained that quite clearly in my speech as to why I think that even with the removal of clause 8F and G, the Minister will still have all the powers he needs to stem hostile foreign interference.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
sentences.text: I mentioned that clause 7, which defines what public interest is, already gives the Minister the power, in the public interest, to take actions if it is necessary to ensure the public health, public finances, public safety, public tranquility, public peace and public order.

sections.label: Public Order Act amendments
sections.summary: The Public Order Act as amended in 2017 covers foreign organisations and participation in activities directed towards a political end in physical spaces in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
sentences.text: The Public Order Act as amended in 2017 deals with foreign organisation and participation in activities directed towards a political end in physical spaces in Singapore.

sections.label: Comparing Public Order Act and FICA
sections.summary: A speaker notes the Public Order Act has the same clause 7(2)(E) but lacks clause 7F on foreign interference directed towards a political end.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
sentences.text: He cited as an example and I would read out clause D – "to prevent incitement of feelings of enmity, hatred or ill will between different groups of people in Singapore".

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
sentences.text: I would point out that the Public Order Act has exactly the same clause 7(2)(E).

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
sentences.text: I think the construct of the Public Order Act and FICA are essentially the same and I do not see why the Workers' Party, who had no issue four years ago, should have the issue today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
sentences.text: But the Public Order Act does not have clause 7F – to prevent any foreign interference directed towards a political end in Singapore.

sections.label: Agreement on Bill's aim
sections.summary: Both sides of the House agree on the Bill's aim, on intrusive powers subject to checks and balances, and on public interest under clause 7.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Both sides of the House are aligned with the aim of the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The hon Leader of the Opposition agreed that intrusive powers may have to be vested with the Minister to deal with this scourge of foreign interference, subject, of course, to checks and balances, which I will come to later.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Both also agree on what constitutes public interest under clause 7 of the Bill.

sections.label: Consensus on clauses 17 and 18
sections.summary: There is broad consensus on criminalising conduct amounting to foreign interference and influence operations under clauses 17 and 18.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: On the issue of criminalising conduct amounting to foreign interference and influence operations under clauses 17 and 18, there is broad consensus.

sections.label: Consensus on political donations provisions
sections.summary: The House has consensus on political donations provisions, election-period declarations by politically significant persons, and disclosures under clauses 78 and 79.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I understand that MHA had earlier indicated that it had intended to do this based on its response dated 25 September 2021 to queries from The Straits Times.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: There is consensus in this House on the provisions dealing with political donations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: There is full consensus to impose on politically significant persons during election period, a requirement that they declare that they are not subject to foreign influence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: There is broad consensus to require these persons to make disclosures of any dealing with/or on behalf of foreign principals or foreign political organisations under clauses 78 and 79, even if the Acts are not directed towards a political end in Singapore, as well as benefits received from these principals.

sections.label: Disclosure of directives
sections.summary: A speaker agrees with Mr Perera that directives be made public, noting the Bill already requires subjects to make disclosure conspicuously.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The hon Member, Mr Perera suggested that such directives be made public.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I agree but I think the suggestion is already present in the current version of the Bill which specifically provides that the subjects of the directives must make disclosure conspicuously.

sections.label: MHA statement on countermeasures
sections.summary: The speaker understands MHA issued a statement on making public countermeasures issued against PSPs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In this regard, I understand MHA had issued a statement on making public such countermeasures issued against PSPs.

sections.label: Appeals and judicial review
sections.summary: The Bill proposes appeals to the Reviewing Tribunal and the Minister with limited judicial review by the Supreme Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Under the Bill, it is proposed that appeals made to the Reviewing Tribunal and the Minister with limited judicial review by the Supreme Court.

sections.label: Minister accountable for foreign interference
sections.summary: The Minister must be held responsible and accountable through the political process for countering foreign interference affecting public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: That, in the scheme of things, was not desirable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It is preferable, when it comes to assessment of what action is to be taken, to counter foreign interference affecting public interest, the Minister must be held responsible and accountable through the political process.

sections.label: Checks and balances in FICA
sections.summary: The speaker views FICA's appellate process, judicial review and ministerial accountability as sufficient checks and balances, not unlimited Executive power.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Similarly, having regard to the subject matter of FICA, establishment of the appellate process in the Bill to set up the Review Tribunal and the preservation of the Supreme Court's powers of judicial review on the issue of procedure as well as when there is an excess of jurisdiction and political accountability of the Minister to our people, I am similarly of the view that there are sufficient checks and balances in place for FICA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The Bill does not confer unlimited power to the Executive, which is a concern of the hon Leader of Opposition.

sections.label: Reviewing Tribunal chairperson appointment
sections.summary: The speaker says the President should consult the Chief Justice in deciding the Reviewing Tribunal chairman, as under Article 151(2).

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The Reviewing Tribunal deals with appeals against an authorisation of a Part III direction.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I note it is contemplated that the chairperson of the Reviewing Tribunal must be a Supreme Court Judge.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: To me, the President should be consulting the Chief Justice, who heads our Judiciary in deciding who should be the chairman.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This is the case under Article 151(2) of the Constitution which provides the chairman and two members of the Advisory Board which deals with preventive detention under the ISA shall be appointed by the President after consulting the Chief Justice.

sections.label: Minister may not follow advice
sections.summary: Under clause 102, the Minister may appoint an Advisory Committee for consultation but may not follow the advice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: To clause 102, I note that the Minister may appoint an Advisory Committee for consultation purposes but he may not follow the advice.

sections.label: Foreign principals and ouster clause
sections.summary: A Member asks whether the Bill introduces an ouster clause, citing a quotation on each generation finding its own equilibrium.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: These discussions must enjoy the most important freedom of all, that they be free of interference from foreign principals who ought to have no voice in this House.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I just have one question for the hon Member Mr Murali Pillai and that pertains to the reference he made in his speech about his earlier Adjournment Motion on the sunlight of scrutiny and I will repeat the quotation where the hon Member says, "It is important for each generation of political leaders and people to find their own equilibrium of what our people would accept without question, under what circumstances and towards what ends." Would the Member not agree that the Bill in question introduces an ouster clause.

sections.label: FICA equilibrium and national security
sections.summary: The Member says FICA deals with national security, does not contemplate detention without trial, and its targeted powers match the ISA equilibrium.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: I found instructive, the speech made by Prof Jayakumar about why the powers dealing with national security should be sited with the political leaders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: So, in my personal view, the equilibrium is still the same vis-a-vis FICA because here, we are dealing with issues of national security.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: Additionally, I would add that FICA does not contemplate detention without trial.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: And the powers of FICA is actually quite targeted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: And as I said earlier in my speech, the focus of FICA is to give targeted powers so that you could better deal with national interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: So, in those circumstances, I would say, having regard to the fact that this is an area that has been traversed and the need to provide targeted directives, the equilibrium that we have in ISA would be the equilibrium that I am comfortable with vis-a-vis FICA and there is no contradiction.

sections.label: Anticipatory directions and judicial review
sections.summary: Section 21 lets the Minister give anticipatory directions on suspicion of preparing foreign-principal online activity, and these decisions are not subject to judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For example, section 21 allows the Minister to give anticipatory directions even when the Minister only suspects or has reason to believe that the person is “preparing for, or planning to undertake, online communications activity by or on behalf of a foreign principal”.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The substance of these decisions under the Bill are not subject to judicial review.

sections.label: Definition of Part 4 PSP
sections.summary: A Part 4 PSP is a person or organisation whose activities are directed in part towards a political end in Singapore and faces countermeasures.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the Bill, a Part 4 PSP is a person or organisation whose activities are directed in part towards a political end in Singapore and the Competent Authority opines that it would be in the public interest to impose countermeasures on the entity.

sections.label: Broad foreign principal definition
sections.summary: Section 4 defines foreign principal broadly, including foreigners who are Permanent Residents, and the Member urges guarding against discriminatory legislation and loss of public trust.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Third, section 4 has defined the meaning of “foreign principal” very broadly to capture any and everything that is remotely foreign in nature, regardless of whether such foreign nature is political or government-related or has a public interest.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: A foreign principal includes a foreigner even if he or she is a Permanent Resident of this country.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This is understandable, as foreign interferences may masquerade as normal foreign entities when in essence they are not.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: However, I would like to caution and remind, in the wake of these broad definitions and this House's very recent extensive debates on foreign manpower and CECA, to guard against inadvertently enacting legislation that is potentially discriminatory in nature.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This may have unintended effects on Singapore’s reputation as a hub for global trade and investments that upholds its constitutional values of equality and fairness.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: A balance must be struck and its consequences understood as it also has a bearing on the trust Singaporeans may have in the Government and its systems.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This is something I recognise and that no one can deny.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: However, I do hope that in the implementation of this Act, we do not inadvertently lose public trust, discourage local political discourse or advocacy, or affect Singapore’s reputation as an open trading hub.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: In 2018, the Select Committee of Online Falsehood, which comprises of members from both sides of this House, concluded that “this phenomenon (of foreign interference) is real and a serious problem in Singapore,” and that the “Committee received evidence that state-sponsored information operations have been carried out against Singapore” and the Committee provided 22 recommendations which included implementing specific countermeasures to combat state-sponsored disinformation operations.

sections.label: IPS survey on digital literacy
sections.summary: An IPS survey found low digital literacy, with 6 in 10 respondents believing false information and over two-thirds trusting a manipulated news article.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Unfortunately, a recent IPS survey also found that our digital literacy rates are worryingly low with 6 in 10 respondents believing false information to be true and found that no one is immune to false information regardless of age, socio-economic status and educational background.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: The IPS study also found that more than two-thirds of over 2,000 respondents trusted a manipulated "news article" presented to them as part of the study.

sections.label: Foreign interference laws abroad
sections.summary: Australia passed foreign interference laws in 2018 and the European Commission proposes a Digital Services Act regulating online platforms.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: For example, in June 2018, Australia passed laws targeting foreign interference in politics and other domestic affairs and the European Commission is proposing a new Digital Services Act which will, among other things, regulate online platforms by transposing what is already illegal offline to the online space.

sections.label: Businesses fear discussing policies
sections.summary: Foreign businesses and MNCs worry that discussing policy impact may breach the law, but the Minister said such discussions do not meet the threshold.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Rightfully, foreign businesses and MNCs are concerned that such discussions on the impact of our policies on their businesses may run them foul of the law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: I am glad to hear that Minister has reiterated that discussions of this nature does not meet the threshold to be foul of the law.

sections.label: IPS digital literacy survey
sections.summary: An Institute of Policy Studies survey found a low digital literacy rate, with two-thirds of respondents believing a manipulated article.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: A survey by the Institute of Policy Studies, or IPS, found that our digital literacy rate was low, with two-thirds of respondents believing in a manipulated article.

sections.label: Foreign state fake accounts protest
sections.summary: In a United States case, a foreign-state organisation used fake accounts promoting Islamic objectives and anti-Islam messages to start a protest against an Islamic library.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: In one case in the United States, an organisation from a foreign state used fake accounts that promote Islamic objectives, as well as fake accounts that spread anti-Islam messages, in order to start a protest against the building of an Islamic library – at the same time and place!

sections.label: Anonymous accounts on Singapore stance
sections.summary: In 2018 and 2019, during airspace and maritime disputes, anonymous accounts made online comments to create fake opposition against Singapore's stance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: For example, in 2018 and 2019, amidst disputes with neighbouring countries over airspace and maritime issues, online comments on social media were found to be made by anonymous accounts aimed at creating fake opposition against Singapore's stance.

sections.label: Select Committee recommendations and safeguards
sections.summary: Since 2018 the Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehood made 22 recommendations, including countermeasures against state-sponsored disinformation, and strong safeguards are needed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: (In English): In summary, Mr Speaker, Sir, since 2018, the Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehood provided 22 recommendations, which included implementing specific countermeasures to combat state-sponsored disinformation operations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Our status as an open economy attracting investments globally implies that we must balance the needs of all stakeholders while putting forward our national interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: We need to enact strong safeguards to protect our national sovereignty and security, protect our social cohesion and protect our democratic institutions.

sections.label: Updating laws against new threats
sections.summary: It states that laws must be updated to deal with new threats, and that many countries have done so and Singapore must too.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: In an increasingly digitised world and given Singapore's global interconnectedness, it is necessary to update our laws from time to time to deal with the new threats that may infiltrate our shores and destabilise or divide us.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Many countries like the US, Australia, New Zealand, Germany and India have done so in various forms in recent years and so must we.

sections.label: Preventative mechanism against foreign interference
sections.summary: It states Singapore is not the first country to have a preventative mechanism against foreign interference, citing the US, Australia, India and Israel.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Singapore is not the first country to put in place a preventative mechanism to prevent foreign interference.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Many countries such as the US, Australia, India and Israel have different types of legal and administrative means to deter foreign interference.

sections.label: Medals and awards to businessmen
sections.summary: It asks the Minister for his view on medals, honorary degrees and awards conferred to Singapore businessmen by overseas governments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Lastly, I would like to ask the Minister for his view on the medals, honorary degrees and awards conferred to Singapore businessmen by overseas governments.

sections.label: Support for the Bill
sections.summary: It notes some Singaporean businessmen or enterprises receive awards or medals from the local government, and states support for the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Some Singaporean businessmen or enterprises will also receive awards or medals from the local government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: (In English): Sir, notwithstanding the points above, I support the Bill.

sections.label: Pritam Singh cites Albert Dicey
sections.summary: It states Mr Pritam Singh cites jurist Albert Dicey on separation of powers and checks and balances on executive power.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Pritam Singh cites the jurist Albert Dicey to remind us of the doctrine of separation of powers and that the rule of law requires a system of checks and balances on the exercise of executive power.

sections.label: Risks in overall legal landscape
sections.summary: It asks how risks are dealt with in the overall legal landscape and whether Mr Singh and Ms He suggest doing away with the ISA, CLTPA and Land Acquisition Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: How are the risks being dealt with in the context of the overall legal landscape?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, listening to Mr Singh and Ms He, does that mean that they also suggest we do away with the ISA, the CLTPA, the Land Acquisition Act and various other pieces of legislation?

sections.label: Workers' Party position on laws
sections.summary: Taking the Workers' Party's position to its extreme would require doing away with the CLTPA, ISA, MRHA and Land Acquisition Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If the Workers' Party’s position is taken to its extreme, as I have said, we would have to do away with the CLTPA, the ISA, the MRHA and the Land Acquisition Act.

sections.label: Judicial process and sensitive intelligence
sections.summary: A judicial process will not be appropriate where reliance is heavy on sensitive intelligence and collaboration with foreign counterparts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: A judicial process will not be appropriate in matters where we rely heavily on sensitive intelligence and collaboration with foreign counterparts.

sections.label: Tribunal appeal and merits review
sections.summary: The Tribunal can consider any appeal against a Part 3 Direction and review the merits, not just procedural compliance or legality.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Tribunal can consider any appeal brought against a Part 3 Direction and there can be a review of the merits of the decision.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is not confined to procedural compliance or legality.

sections.label: Tribunal powers over Minister
sections.summary: The Tribunal can overrule the Minister's decision, and clause 95(2) insulates its members from pressure on salary and terms.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Let us please not insult our High Court Judges.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And this Tribunal has powers to overrule the Minister’s decision.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
