sentences.text: The Tribunal has been, as I said, expressly vested with the powers to override the Minister's decision and it is useful to point out clause 95(2) of the Bill insulates the members of the Reviewing Tribunal from pressure and states very clearly that the Minister cannot reduce the salary and terms of office once they are appointed by the President.

sections.label: Bill page length correction
sections.summary: The Bill is 189 pages long, not 249 pages as some have pointed out.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: For those who have pointed out that the Bill is 249 pages long; in the interest of accuracy, it is 189 pages long.

sections.label: Updating powers for Internet age
sections.summary: The Bill updates powers for the Internet age, and given the threats there is a clear and present danger justifying acting now.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Information forces are seen as a fourth branch of armed service.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This Bill is about updating our powers to ensure that they are fit for the Internet age.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Given the threats, we think there is a clear and present danger that justifies us acting now.

sections.label: FICA and overseas activities
sections.summary: FICA will not stop individuals, businesses and organisations in Singapore from building overseas partnerships, soliciting overseas business, networking, sourcing donations, discussing policies or supporting charities.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: FICA will not stop individuals, businesses and organisations in Singapore from building overseas partnerships, soliciting overseas business, networking with foreigners, sourcing for donations, discussing government policies or political matters that affect their businesses with foreign colleagues or business partners or supporting charities.

sections.label: Arrest powers and offences
sections.summary: The Bill's arrest powers relate to specific offences proven in Court beyond reasonable doubt, and there is no detention without trial.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In the Bill, the powers of arrest relate to specific offences which need to be proven in Court like any other offence, and proven beyond reasonable doubt.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There is no detention without trial in this Bill.

sections.label: No detention without trial
sections.summary: The speaker tells Mr Leong there is no power for detention without trial in this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, we are talking about, I think, completely different things.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I can tell Mr Leong, there is no power for detention without trial in this Bill.

sections.label: Reviewing Tribunal standing
sections.summary: The Reviewing Tribunal will be a standing Tribunal.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Reviewing Tribunal will be a standing Tribunal.

sections.label: HIC directions and PSP designations
sections.summary: HIC directions are authorised by the Minister, and PSP designations and countermeasures by a civil servant within MHA.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: HIC directions authorised by the Minister and PSP designations and countermeasures by a civil servant within MHA.

sections.label: Designation and appeals details
sections.summary: Operational details on the designation and appeals process are still being worked out and will be introduced in subsidiary legislation and as Regulations.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Operational details on the designation and appeals process are still being worked out and will be introduced in subsidiary legislation and as Regulations.

sections.label: Advisory committee appointments made public
sections.summary: The Minister has no issues with making advisory committee appointments public, in reply to a question on gazetting and public awareness.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Murali Pillai asked if the appointments to the advisory committee to advise the Minister on PSP appeals will be gazetted and make public and how would the public know that the Minister is not following the advisory committee's advice.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We have no issues with making the appointments public.

sections.label: Part 3 directions published online
sections.summary: All Part 3 directions except the Technical Assistance Direction will be published on a publicly accessible website.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: All Part 3 directions, except for the Technical Assistance Direction, will be published on a website accessible to the public.

sections.label: Intentionality in HIC offence
sections.summary: Intentionality cannot be removed from the offence elements, so the threshold is set at a reasonable level such as 'is or is likely to'.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The starting point is indeed we want to make it an offence to conduct or abet a HIC.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But we cannot remove intentionality from the offence elements, otherwise we will end up making criminals out of Singaporeans who unknowingly aid an HIC by sharing content without knowing better.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: A deliberate perpetrator may of course deny, which is why we need to set the offence threshold at a reasonable level, "is or is likely to", for example.

sections.label: Overseas Singaporean designation practicality
sections.summary: Delaying designation of an overseas Singaporean not planning to return may not be practical until an opportunity to be heard is given.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If the designated individual is a Singaporean based overseas and not planning on returning to Singapore, it may not be practical to delay his or her designation until he or she is given an opportunity to be heard.

sections.label: Further measures against foreign interference
sections.summary: Mr Christopher de Souza asked MHA about deterring foreign interference, and the reply said further measures need consideration after the Select Committee findings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: Mr Christopher de Souza filed a cut, asking MHA what it would do to deter foreign interference in our domestic affairs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: It goes on for about a page, and right at the end, she says, "Given the experience of other countries, we need to consider further measures".

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: This is post-Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods' findings, post some other seminars that have been referred to.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: And she says, "We need to consider further measures to guard against foreign subversion, what levels of transparency, support, leadership are appropriate for home and the public has to play a big part in this to shape proposals and to give safeguards the strongest support".

sections.label: FICA judicial review grounds limited
sections.summary: Under FICA's limited judicial review clause, illegality and irrationality are not grounds for review, only procedural impropriety.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: The Minister in taking his decision can arguably be made to realise that if his decision is so unreasonable that one look at the facts will show that he could never have considered the detainee a threat, then his decision should be reversed by the Courts." Insofar as FICA is concerned and as it is drafted with the limited judicial review clause, what we are taking away is precisely what the Minister was warning about in 1989.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: Illegality, irrationality are not grounds for judicial review consideration in this Bill, only procedural impropriety.

sections.label: FICA foreign funding PSE question
sections.summary: Asks whether a Singapore NGO classified as a Politically Significant Entity would be barred from accepting foreign funding under FICA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: They are prepared to extend funding to anyone.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: Now, one reading of FICA, by virtue of a clause 8(f) and (g) and even (e) perhaps, will suggest that, this Singapore NGO could be classified as a Politically Significant Entity (PSE).

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: My question is, will such a PSE be barred at the first instance, at the baseline, from continuing to accept foreign funding.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: At the baseline, I believe it says you cannot accept impermissible donations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I believe the Bill in clause 55 tells you what a permissible donor is.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: Are we to read that in the opposite, as in everybody who is out of that range is an impermissible donor?

sections.label: Whole-of-society major attack warning
sections.summary: States that whole-of-society is not the end and a major attack will be faced at some point.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But if we talk about whole-of-society, this is not the end.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We will face a major attack at some point.

sections.label: High Court FICA model
sections.summary: States that going to the High Court for FICA is not a better model.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Going to the High Court for FICA is not a better model.

sections.label: Refusing to change mind
sections.summary: Says a man who looks at facts and the real world but refuses to change his mind is stupid or ideological.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If a man looks at the facts, the real world and refuses to change his mind, he is either stupid or he is ideological.

sections.label: People under CL comparison
sections.summary: Asks to compare the number of people under the CL today with the number 10 years ago.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Look at the number of people under the CL today compared to the number of people under the CL even 10 years ago.

sections.label: Singapore versus Indian land acquisition
sections.summary: Asks whether Singapore would be where it is if every land acquisition matter went to the Supreme Court as in India.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Would we in Singapore be where we are if we had taken the Indian approach and every matter goes up to the Supreme Court on land acquisition and it takes years to deal with it?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, I saw the genius in the adaptations that our system has made or the founding generation has made, being very strict in building up our judiciary.

sections.label: rule of law and judiciary ranking
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether without commitment to the rule of law the judiciary would be ranked as it is today.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If we do not have a commitment to the rule of law, do you think our judiciary will be ranked as it is today?

sections.label: order and rule of law foundations
sections.summary: The speaker says these were built on bringing order first and ensuring the law and commitment to the rule of law are present.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: All of these were built up with the foundations of bringing order first and making sure that the law and the commitment to the rule of law are there.

sections.label: drafting legislation with AGC
sections.summary: The speaker says he and his officers drafted this with the AGC, some parts he wished were different, describing the legislation as a toy gun against people armed with bazookas.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, as I sat with my officers and drafted this and with the AGC, yes, there were parts that I wished were different.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But that threat we face, as I said, are people armed with bazookas and I described this legislation as a toy gun.

sections.label: foreign funding at designation onset
sections.summary: The speaker says at designation onset a PSE only declares foreign donors and funding sources, and ceasing funding is required only when certain conditions are met.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: Will it therefore be required to cease the foreign funding at the onset of the designation?

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: So, the short answer to the question is no.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: At the onset of designation, the PSE will only be required to declare the foreign donors and where the funding is coming from.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: Only when there are reasons and it meets certain conditions will it be required to step up the countermeasures, the further measures to require the NGOs to then beyond declaring, to have to cease the funding, only when certain conditions are met.

sections.label: sensitive information from partners
sections.summary: The speaker says their assessment was that much evidence relied on would be highly sensitive information from partners outside.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The reason is, our assessment was that here, a lot of the evidence we will rely on would probably be based on highly sensitive information that comes from our partners; by definition, partners meaning from outside.

sections.label: malign foreign state influence question
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether, referring to the 2018-2019 events, he continues to believe there was malign foreign state influence in that case.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: The first is to ask if in referring to the events of 2018-2019, whether he continues to believe that there was indeed malign foreign state influence in that case.

sections.label: Reasonable suspicion versus probable cause
sections.summary: The passage notes the Bill excludes judicial review, making precedent advisory, and that reasonable suspicion allows more limited actions than probable cause.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: Does this always refer to the term reasonable suspicion, a point that I believe Members of Zhulkarnain and Murali also mentioned.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: Second, while we do have a long history of, as other Members have said, of using this term in case law, lest we forget the Bill as it stands, does exclude judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: So, any such precedent strikes me as a largely advisory and informative rather than binding.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: And third, I think it is worth remembering that the types of actions typically afforded by reasonable suspicion tend to be much more limited than those associated with probable cause.

sections.label: Facebook Sinhalese calls to kill Muslims
sections.summary: The passage states that in Sri Lanka around 2016 or 2017, Sinhalese on Facebook called to gather and kill Muslims.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We were watching all the different media that was used.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Now, in Sri Lanka, and I think this was 2017 or 2016, on Facebook, Sinhalese were calling to gather together to go and kill Muslims.

sections.label: Facebook response on community standards
sections.summary: The passage states Facebook told him this does not affect our community standards.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Facebook told him this does not affect our community standards.

sections.label: Facebook and New Zealand mosque livestream
sections.summary: The passage states Facebook said the New Zealand mosque attacker's livestream did not breach its community standards until uproar made it reverse course.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: When attacker in the New Zealand mosque was killing people and livestreaming his attack, Facebook said it did not breach its community standards and it felt that attack should continue to be livestreamed, until there was such a furore and uproar that they reversed course.

sections.label: Spike in Mandarin targeted messages
sections.summary: The passage states a sudden spike in activity on platforms targeting specific messages for the Mandarin speaking population was a clear indication.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But we noticed activity, we draw certain lines.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We have people and they have come to the conclusion that the sudden spike in activity on a variety of platforms, specifically targeted for specific messages to be absorbed by our Mandarin speaking population was a very clear indication.

sections.label: High Court Judge as check
sections.summary: The passage states a strong check is the appointment of a High Court Judge with extensive powers to deal with a clear and present threat.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Your question is, do you give the power and what are the checks you put in.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, we have put in, we think, a strong check through the appointment of a High Court Judge with extensive powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We have drafted this to deal with a very large threat which is clear and present here.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It has happened, it is happening all around us and it will happen to us.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is not for nothing that the French study Singapore and showed it as a test case or one of the case studies.

sections.label: Public consultation and FICA effectiveness
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the Minister should postpone the Bill due to insufficient public consultation and whether FICA is effective.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: That is not the way the law should be implemented.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: So, since there is not enough consultation of the general public, should the Minister not consider postponing the passage of the Bill?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: The second question, is FICA effective in protecting us much more than all the resources and the laws we have before this?

sections.label: Tribunal appointment and judicial review
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the Minister appoints the Tribunal under FICA and why judicial review cannot be done here.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: The Tribunal is appointed by the Minister, right, under this FICA?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Two, if judicial review can be done in other country, even with respect to national security issues, why can we not do it?

sections.label: Tribunal appointment and independence
sections.summary: The Tribunal is appointed by the President on Cabinet advice and headed by a High Court Judge with security of tenure.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Tribunal is appointed by the President, on the advice of the Cabinet.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is headed by a High Court Judge, who has security of tenure, and he is a Judge of the Supreme Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: He does not owe any obligation to the Government.

sections.label: France attackers known to security forces
sections.summary: The speaker states that in France, 80% of the attackers were known to the security forces.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If you take France, I said 80% of the attackers were known to the security forces.

sections.label: Minister response time limit commitment
sections.summary: The Minister cannot commit to a time limit to respond but commits to doing so as expeditiously as possible.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: On the first question, 30 days and whether there will be a time limit.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is difficult to commit to a time limit for the Minister to respond, simply because it depends on the facts and the kind of evidence that needs to be assessed.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But what we can commit to is that it will be done as expeditiously as possible.

sections.label: CPIB investigation and higher authority
sections.summary: The speaker says CPIB can investigate anyone including the Prime Minister and reports to a higher independent authority.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Or is it actually going to affect the performance of the Government in such a way that actually trust will go down?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think Mr Perera must be aware the CPIB can investigate anyone including the Prime Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: When the CPIB wants to investigate the Prime Minister, there is a higher authority they report to, independently.

sections.label: Second reading vote recorded
sections.summary: The Clerk records 75 Ayes, 11 Noes and two Abstentions, and the Bill is read a second time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: The Clerk will now proceed to record the votes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: There are 75 "Ayes", 11 "Noes" and two "Abstentions".

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: The Bill has now been read a second time.

sections.label: Bill not hybrid
sections.summary: The Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Bill applies to the public at large, so it is not a hybrid Bill and Standing Order No 68 does not apply.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: The Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Bill now before the House applies to the public at large and does not specifically apply to an individual.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: It is therefore, not a hybrid Bill and Standing Order No 68 does not apply.

sections.label: Amendments to clauses withdrawn
sections.summary: A Member withdraws amendments to clauses 81, 84 and 85, expecting the Minister's clause 116 amendment to cover the same ground.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: The Minister earlier on verbally referred to that amendment and in the expectation that the House will pass the amendment to clause 116 that the Minister for Home Affairs has proposed which, in my opinion will substantively cover the same ground as covered by my amendments to clauses 81, 84 and 85, I would like to withdraw those three amendments with the proviso of this comment that in relation to Technical Assistance Directives, the Minister shared that these are difficult to publicise due to the sensitivity of investigations being ongoing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: So, that is just something I would like to express but my intention here today is withdraw my amendments to clauses 81, 84 and 85 in my name in the Order Paper Supplement, for the reasons I have given.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The second amendment in page 165, lines 28, 29 and 30: to leave out "may prepare a notice informing about any designation made under Part 4, or any", and to insert "must prepare a notice informing about every Part 3 direction (except that technical assistance direction) given, every designation made under Part 4, or every".

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The third amendment in page 166, line 3: after "fact of", to insert "the giving of Part 3 direction,".
